title: H02: Daily melEDI patterns across sites and people
text:
The preregistered hypothesis was:

“Within-participant variance in hourly melanopic EDI, with participants nested in sites, exceeds variance between sites.”

The preregistered model was:
Metric ~ Site +
  s(Time, by = Site, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(Participant, Time, bs = "fs")
The scientific question is whether daily patterns of melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) differ among sites, how much people within a site differ from one another, and whether those within-site differences are larger than the differences among sites.






NoteAnswer in brief



Near-eye daily patterns differed among sites (\chi^2= 474.93, 96 degrees of freedom, false-discovery-rate (FDR)-adjusted p = <0.001). Participant curves plus participant-day shifts were 1.99 (95% CI 1.29 to 4.77) times as dispersed as site curves. In the conditional Shapley analysis, those two participant-level blocks received 9.49 (95% CI 5.77 to 21.81) times as much in-sample model-fit credit as the site-pattern block. Chest measurements gave the same combined ordering.

title: H02: Daily melEDI patterns across sites and people
text:
What was analysed
The near-eye sensor position is primary because it measures light closer to the eye, but it is not a direct retinal measurement. The chest sensor position is analysed separately as complementary evidence and is not a measure of ocular exposure; the two placements are never pooled. During reported sleep, both positions characterize the bedside light environment rather than light at their nominal worn position.
A participant-day is one participant’s observations on one local calendar date. Counts of participant-days therefore describe repeated recorded days, not additional independent participants.
The model used local wall-clock time to describe the daily pattern. True UTC time determined observation ordering. A 30-minute bin entered the model when at least 15 of its 30 one-minute melEDI values were valid. Missing, unsupported, non-wear, and out-of-range values remained missing, not zero. Repeated fall-back clock bins retained their fold provenance; residual sequences were reset at each participant-day, after any elapsed-time discontinuity, and around a wall-clock outcome without a one-to-one true-time coordinate.
Terms used below

A nonlinear GAM analysis uses a generalized additive model (GAM), which allows the association with local clock time to bend across the day rather than forcing it to follow a straight line.
The model uses log10(melEDI + 0.1 lx). A back-transformed curve applies the inverse transformation and returns to melEDI in lux.
Participant and participant-day smooths represent fitted variation that remains among people or recorded days after the time and site patterns have been considered.

Autocorrelation means adjacent 30-minute residuals can remain more alike than residuals farther apart. The AR(1) structure represents this dependence as strongest for adjacent observations and weaker at longer lags.
A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) gives uncertainty at one displayed clock time. It is not a simultaneous band for the full day and does not multiplicity-control every red segment in a daily curve.

Shapley allocation averages a model component’s contribution over all orders in which components could be added, allocating shared fitted-model information rather than counting it repeatedly.

The complete registration-change record appears in the detailed analysis record.

title: H02: Daily melEDI patterns across sites and people
text:
Model
The daily patterns were estimated with a nonlinear GAM analysis. This model combines a curved time-of-day pattern with structured departures for sites, participants, and participant-days while retaining the repeated-measures structure.
The exact Wilkinson formula was:
response ~
  s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +
  s(participant_day, bs = "re")
Here, response is \log_{10}(\mathrm{melEDI}+0.1\ \mathrm{lx}). The first term is the global time effect, which is the site-average daily curve: it gives every site equal weight and joins smoothly at midnight. The sz term estimates how each site’s curve departs from that site-average curve; the departures sum to zero, so no reference site is required. The participant smooth represents remaining differences in daily shape among people after the reported time and site patterns are considered. Participant identifiers are site-prefixed, so people remain nested within sites. The participant-day random effect represents remaining day-to-day level shifts within participants after those patterns are considered; it shifts an entire fitted day up or down without changing its shape.
Only the global time effect is explicitly cyclic. The default time marginals inside the sz site term and fs participant term are not forced to meet at midnight. A fully cyclic formulation is therefore included as a model-form sensitivity.
Because adjacent 30-minute residuals can remain more similar than residuals farther apart, the model was fitted with mgcv::bam() under fREML and a boundary-aware AR(1) working correlation. Site curves and their pointwise 95% CIs were obtained from the fitted linear-predictor matrix and full coefficient covariance. Each interval describes uncertainty at one clock time; it is not a simultaneous band across the day. Smoothing parameters are treated as fixed in these intervals. gratia was used for residual appraisal and for the concurvity model check; concurvity is overlap among nonlinear model terms that makes their separate contributions harder to distinguish.
Quantities used to compare sites and people
The first comparison describes the spread of the fitted curves. On a common 48-bin clock grid,

V_{\mathrm{site}} =
\frac{1}{48}\sum_b
\operatorname{Var}_{s}\{\hat f_s(t_b)\},

and participant-curve variation is the within-site variance among participant curves over the same clock grid, averaged across sites with each site receiving equal weight. Participant-day variation uses the same site-average weighting for the variance of day-specific intercept contributions. Their ratios compare fitted curve dispersion on the transformed modelling scale. They are not proportions of response variance and are not “variance explained.”
The second comparison asks which model block contributes more to in-sample fit. The global time effect is retained in every model. Site pattern, participant pattern, and participant-day shift are then included in every possible combination. For each block, the conditional Shapley allocation is its average increase in row-weighted in-sample R^2 across all possible orders of entry. This allocates shared fitted-model information without counting it repeatedly. It describes conditional in-sample model-fit relevance, not causal importance or cross-validated predictive importance.
Both sets of 95% confidence intervals use 2,000 hierarchical cluster resamples: sites, participants within sampled sites, and participant-days within sampled participants. The fitted curve contributions or fitted subset models are held fixed. The intervals therefore describe cluster-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted smoothing structure.

title: H02: Daily melEDI patterns across sites and people
text:
Sensitivity to other analytical choices
The table changes one substantive choice at a time where possible. The gap-timing-unaware dataset sensitivity changes the prepared 30-minute dataset while retaining the model specification. It is the predefined data-preparation sensitivity. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules, but the timing of the remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For contrast, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset because its preparation uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant to the metric; it is called simply the primary dataset elsewhere in this report. The fully cyclic basis sensitivity changes the site and participant time bases so those deviations also meet at midnight. The placement-matched sensitivities change the fitted sample by restricting near-eye and chest fits to the same participant-day-clock observations. The complementary chest analysis changes sensor position while retaining the selected formula and implementation. A separate non-cyclic global-time basis check changed only the global time basis from cyclic cubic to thin plate; residual model checks did not materially improve and midnight continuity worsened.

The participant-plus-day/site ratio remained above one under every reported choice. The point estimate changed from 1.99 in the primary near-eye analysis to 1.92 in the gap-timing-unaware dataset and 1.89 under the fully cyclic model. On the exact placement-matched sample it was 1.54 near-eye and 1.75 chest. The participant-only ratio was less stable: its interval included one in the chest and placement-matched analyses. The strongest reproducible conclusion is therefore that participant-specific patterns together with day-to-day shifts vary more than site patterns; the participant-pattern-only contrast is less certain outside the full near-eye sample.

title: H02: Daily melEDI patterns across sites and people
text:
Interpretation
The daily profile is dominated by the global time effect. After that pattern was considered, the fitted variation among people and their recorded days was larger than the fitted variation among sites. People within the same site showed more distinct fitted daily patterns than the average differences among site curves, especially when day-to-day level shifts were included.
Two complementary summaries support that interpretation:

fitted participant-plus-day curves were about twice as dispersed as site curves in the primary near-eye analysis; and
participant pattern plus participant-day shift received about 9.5 times as much conditional in-sample R^2 credit as site pattern.

Those statements have different denominators and should not be numerically combined. The first compares model-implied curve spread. The second allocates in-sample model fit. Neither is a causal effect, a population-wide fraction of variance, or a guarantee of out-of-sample prediction.
Limitations
The site-specific time windows are useful for describing when a fitted site profile departs from the global time effect, but each ribbon is a pointwise 95% CI rather than a simultaneous band. A reader should not interpret every red segment as a separate familywise-controlled discovery. The single confirmatory family contains only the near-eye omnibus site-pattern test, so FDR adjustment leaves its p-value unchanged.
Overall, the model provides a defensible description of mean daily patterns and supports the preregistered ordering when participant-day variation is included. Confidence is tempered by the zero-heavy residual distribution, remaining day-specific serial correlation, high common/site concurvity, only nine near-eye sites, and the conditional rather than model-refitting nature of the bootstrap intervals.

text:
The scientific question was whether daily patterns of melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) differed among sites and whether differences among people within sites were larger than the differences among sites. This page explains which data and code produced the reported H02 result, why each analytical step was needed, and what evidence shows that the processing and model behaved as intended. The companion H02 results report presents the scientific findings.

Why the response was transformed
The fitted response is \log_{10}(\mathrm{melEDI}+0.1\ \mathrm{lx}). The offset retains exact-zero observations and maps them to −1. The transformation compresses a range that extends from darkness to tens of thousands of lux, but it does not make the zero mass disappear. Because this discrete spike is much taller than any bin among the positive measurements, combining both in one histogram hides the shape of the positive distribution. The figure therefore reports the number and percentage of exact zeros separately and uses its vertical scale for positive melEDI observations only.

title: H02 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
3. Model construction
Exact selected formula
scripts/hypotheses/H02/h02_modeling.R contains the fitting functions; h02_contract.R supplies their fixed specification. The exact Wilkinson formula was:
response ~
  s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +
  s(participant_day, bs = "re")
The first smooth is the global time effect: the cyclic daily pattern shared across sites. The sz term estimates site-specific departures that sum to zero. This centres the global time effect equally across sites without making any one site the reference. The participant factor smooth estimates a person-specific daily shape within site. The participant-day random intercept allows an entire fitted day to shift up or down.
Only the global time effect is forced to join at midnight in the primary model. A sensitivity analysis also makes the site and participant deviations cyclic.
Model settings

Show the R code used for this displaytibble::tribble(

What run_h02_analysis.R does
The primary near-eye model is fitted first. Reduced versions without the site pattern, participant pattern, or participant-day intercept are fitted with the same estimated AR parameter to compare model structures. The full structure is retained, and the identical selected structure is then applied to the other seven H02 frames. Each scenario estimates its own boundary-aware AR parameter from its preliminary residuals.
For every fitted scenario, the script writes the selected model, a checkpoint, site-curve predictions, fitted term contributions, residual summaries, and the stored 2,000-draw hierarchical variation bootstrap. The following fit table is read from model_fit_summary.csv; no fit is performed here.

title: H02 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
4. Ordering and residual dependence
Why local time and true time are both needed
Autocorrelation means that adjacent 30-minute residuals can remain more alike than residuals farther apart. The AR(1) structure represents this correlation as strongest for adjacent observations and weaker at longer lags. It must restart wherever two observations are not part of the same continuous recorded sequence.
Local wall-clock time answers the scientific question about time of day. It cannot by itself establish elapsed ordering across daylight-saving folds, gaps, or missing bins. h02_data.R therefore carries the verified true-UTC source-bin links into each model frame, orders observations by true elapsed time, and defines a new residual sequence:

at the start of every participant-day;
after a missing or otherwise discontinuous 30-minute interval; and
on both sides of a wall-clock outcome that has no one-to-one elapsed-time coordinate.

The table is read from the recorded boundary check. “Continuous” rows are ordinary observations inside an existing sequence and are included only to make the denominator visible.

title: H02 analysis preparation and provenance
section: 5. From fitted models to reported quantities
text:
5. From fitted models to reported quantities
Site curves and pointwise intervals
h02_modeling.R and h02_figure4_pointwise.R evaluate the stored model on a common 48-bin clock grid. The global time effect is the site-average curve, an average across sites that gives every site equal weight. A site curve is that global effect plus the site’s sum-to-zero departure. Participant and participant-day terms are set to their reference contributions when constructing site curves. A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes uncertainty at one displayed clock time. It comes from the fitted linear-predictor matrix and coefficient covariance with smoothing parameters held fixed; it is not a simultaneous band for the full day and does not multiplicity-control every red segment. The plotted curves are back-transformed to melEDI in lux for reader interpretation.
build_h02_figure4_replication.R applies the same builder to near-eye and chest models. It reads stored fits and contributions; it does not refit the model. Its principal outputs are:


artifacts/10_figures/H02/figure4_exact_layout_replication.png;

artifacts/10_figures/H02/figure4_exact_layout_replication_chest.png;
matching PDF files; and

artifacts/11_source_data/H02/figure4_exact_layout_source*.rds.
Fitted-curve variation
For every scenario, run_h02_analysis.R extracts the fitted global, site, participant, and participant-day contributions. It then calculates precisely defined curve-dispersion summaries on the modelling scale. Within-site participant and day summaries use site-average weighting, so every site contributes equally.
The stored 95% intervals resample sites, participants within sites, and participant-days within participants 2,000 times. The fitted contributions remain fixed. Thus, the bootstrap describes cluster-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted smooth structure; it is not a model-refitting bootstrap. The stored resampling draws are under artifacts/08_diagnostics/H02/*__variation_bootstrap.rds.
Shapley allocation of fitted-model relevance
run_h02_dominance_analysis.R is intentionally narrower: it runs only for the main all-available near-eye and complementary chest samples. The global time effect is mandatory in all subset models. The script fits every one of the eight possible combinations of site pattern, participant pattern, and participant-day shift, then allocates their increments in row-weighted in-sample R^2 across all orders of entry. This Shapley allocation is the average contribution of a component across all orders in which the components could be added, so shared fitted-model information is allocated rather than counted repeatedly. The implementation is also recorded technically as exact general dominance.
The 2,000-draw hierarchical bootstrap resamples clusters while holding the eight sets of fitted predictions fixed. The calculation is descriptive in-sample relevance, not causal importance and not cross-validated predictive importance. Stored results and execution evidence are under:


artifacts/09_tables/H02/dominance_*.csv;

artifacts/11_source_data/H02/*__dominance_predictions.rds;

artifacts/08_diagnostics/H02/*__dominance_bootstrap.rds; and

artifacts/12_manifests/H02/H02_dominance_manifest.csv.

6. Diagnostics and influence
run_h02_temporal_diagnostics.R reads the stored selected models and model frames. It verifies coefficient rank and convergence, basis dimensions, sum-to-zero constraints, midnight continuity, boundary-aware residual behaviour, formal concurvity, and participant/site influence. gratia is used for the formal concurvity wrapper; mgcv supplies the fitted GAM machinery and core diagnostics.
build_h02_reader_diagnostics.R converts the diagnostic source objects into the compact near-eye and chest figures used in the H02 results report. Neither script changes the selected formula. Key externally produced outputs are:

10. How to audit or extend H02
For a read-only assessment, a reviewer can proceed in four passes:

inspect h02_contract.R and input_hashes.csv to confirm the frozen input and model contract;
compare the descriptive samples and support displays above with sample_counts.csv and the model-frame RDS files;
follow the producing script named in each stage manifest, checking that its recorded inputs and outputs match the intended estimand; and
read the Step 3 report alongside the result tables, diagnostic outputs, and source-data objects rather than attempting to infer results from a figure image alone.

Any proposed change to a shared base artifact or shared preparation rule must return to the coordinating task. A new H02 model choice should be implemented as an explicitly named sensitivity until its estimand, diagnostics, and inheritance consequences for H11 are resolved.






TipReader takeaway



The H02 result was not generated inside a single opaque notebook. It came from a pinned input contract, H02-only model frames, a reusable temporal-model implementation, separate inferential and diagnostic stages, stored cluster-bootstrap evidence, and file-level manifests. This document makes that chain inspectable while leaving the accepted scientific result and its computational artifacts unchanged.

title: How H03–H11 will be reviewed and rebuilt
text:
This workflow applies to H03 through H11. It does not retroactively change the work already underway for H01, H02, or the descriptive tables and figures.
Each hypothesis is completed in four stages:

audit and proposed analysis;
implementation and comparison with V0;
a standalone reader-facing results report; and
a scientific description and provenance record for the result-producing pipeline.

When final inference requires a computation-heavy bootstrap or simulation, the production run is an additional approval gate between Stages 2 and 3. It is not a numbered reporting stage. Work stops after Stages 1 and 2, after any production-computation gate, and after Stage 3 until the author has reviewed the relevant HTML output. Stage 4 begins only after the reader-facing result has been accepted.
One hypothesis task retains responsibility from Stage 1 through Stage 4. It pauses at each gate and resumes in the same task only after explicit author approval; a new task is not created for every stage. This continuity preserves the evidence and reasoning developed during the audit without weakening any approval gate.

section: Terms used in the audit reports
text:
Terms used in the audit reports
V0 analysis means the analysis that produced the submitted manuscript. It includes the methods, code, prepared data, numerical results, figures, tables, and claims used for that submission.
Main analysis means the analysis developed and approved through this audit for the Nature Health submission.
V0-prepared data means the data as prepared for V0, with only objectively demonstrable data errors corrected. Applying the new model implementation to these data is an audit-only data-preparation sensitivity. It is not a second version of the reader-facing analysis.
The final reader-facing document does not use the term V0 and does not describe discarded candidate models or variants considered while developing the analysis.
In Stage 3 and Stage 4, this sensitivity is called the gap-timing-unaware dataset. Its first mention explains that it still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules; the label means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. At that first explanation only, the primary dataset may be described as something that could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset. It is called simply the primary dataset thereafter. Internal scenario identifiers and filenames may retain their established names for provenance.

Verifying the source files
The analysis starts from named, versioned files rather than an informal copy of the data. Two prepared datasets enter the analysis. The primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset because its preparation uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant to the metric. The predefined sensitivity is the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules, but the timing of the remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. This name does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored.

section: 10. How to examine or reproduce H02
text:
10. How to examine or reproduce H02
A reader can examine the analysis in four passes:

inspect h02_contract.R and input_hashes.csv to confirm the frozen input files and model specification;
compare the descriptive samples and support displays above with sample_counts.csv and the model-frame RDS files;
follow the producing script named in each stage manifest, checking that its recorded inputs and outputs match the quantity being estimated; and
read the H02 results report alongside the result tables, diagnostic outputs, and source-data objects rather than attempting to infer results from a figure image alone.

Changes to source data or processing rules should be made before the hypothesis-specific model frames are built and then propagated to every affected analysis. Changing H02 alone would otherwise break comparability with the other hypotheses. Alternative H02 model choices should remain clearly labelled sensitivity analyses until their estimands and diagnostics are established.






TipReader takeaway



The H02 result was not generated inside a single opaque notebook. It came from a verified set of source files, H02-only model frames, a reusable temporal-model implementation, separate inferential and diagnostic stages, stored cluster-bootstrap evidence, and checksummed outputs. This page shows how those pieces connect without changing the reported scientific result.

title: How H03–H11 will be reviewed and rebuilt
section: Scientific analysis preparation and provenance companion
text:
Scientific analysis preparation and provenance companion
After the reader-facing result and its accepted artifacts are fixed, the same hypothesis task creates audit/hypotheses/Hxx/Hxx_analysis_preparation.qmd. This companion is not an additional scientific stage or approval gate. It explains how the accepted result was prepared and how its provenance can be checked without reintroducing V0 comparisons into the result report.
The phrase “Step 4” may be used as internal workflow shorthand, but it never appears in the companion’s title, prose, diagrams, captions, tables, callouts, or website navigation. The companion is written for an ordinary scientific reader, not for someone familiar with coordinator/worker roles, approvals, gates, task ownership, or migration history. Those internal mechanics and irrelevant construction variants are omitted.
The page follows REPORT-007 and the revised H02 exemplar. It explains what data and code produced the result, why each analytical operation was needed, what it contributed, and what evidence shows that it behaved as intended. In analytical order, it covers:

exact verified inputs and their identity, schema, key, content, and value checks;
model-frame and sample construction, exclusions, support, missingness, coverage, transformations, units, and temporal ordering;
exact participants, participant-days, observations or hours, sites, and relevant per-site or category samples;
model construction, central settings, estimands, contrasts, multiplicity, uncertainty, and inference;
convergence, distributional, residual, temporal, influence, and other applicable diagnostics;
registered sensitivity branches; and
the provenance of stored models, resampling results, predictions, figures, tables, diagnostics, source data, manifests, and claims.

The page names the hypothesis-specific scripts or modules in execution order and explains what each reads, why it is separate, and what it produces. Useful compact gt tables and plots show input distributions, support, missingness or coverage, and intermediate quantities. A Mermaid data-to-result diagram is used when it materially clarifies the chain. Technical concepts are explained on first use in specific but plain publication language.

Bounded rendering
An informational note states which bounded identity checks and lightweight descriptive calculations run during rendering and which quantities are read from stored outputs. It does not use warning, important, caution, or danger styling.
Rendering must not refit models, re-estimate autocorrelation, regenerate model predictions, rerun bootstraps or simulations, recompute Shapley analyses, or repeat other expensive scientific computation. Externally generated results need not be recomputed, but their producing scripts and exact output locations are identified.


Displays, source data, and website identity
Tables are readable and split into digestible pieces. Every figure has an informative caption, non-empty alt text, and exact paired source data. Axes use scientifically appropriate scales. Discrete masses such as exact zeros are shown separately when they would compress a continuous distribution, while the page states explicitly whether those observations remained in the fitted model.
The companion and notebooks/hypotheses/Hxx.qmd link to each other. The coordinator adds the companion immediately after the result in the Nature Health render list and navigation only after the source exists. The authoring QMD remains available in the website output and its copied bytes must match the authoring source exactly.
The hypothesis-specific preparation manifest records the source, website QMD copy, HTML, figures, paired source data, scripts, scientific outputs, environment identity, byte sizes, and SHA-256 checksums. It excludes the final worker inventory and any other self-reference that would make the checksum chain circular.


Structural verification and closure
Every hypothesis adds a focused structural test for reader-facing wording, informational callout semantics, reciprocal links and navigation, figure captions and alt text, gt tables, paired source data, bounded executable R chunks, source-copy identity, and manifest coverage. The shared verifier is scripts/pipeline/hypothesis_preparation_provenance_contract.R; each hypothesis extends it with its own required content and expensive function names.
The hypothesis task refreshes its preparation manifest, non-circular worker inventory, tests, and handoff after coordinator-owned website integration. This documentation closure does not reopen an accepted result unless it exposes a substantive discrepancy. The complete contract is recorded in audit/decisions/hypothesis_preparation_provenance_companions.md.

title: How H03–H11 will be reviewed and rebuilt
section: Optional production-computation gate between Stages 2 and 3

title: How H03–H11 will be reviewed and rebuilt
text:
Stage 3: Standalone reader-facing hypothesis report
The final notebooks/hypotheses/Hxx.qmd stands on its own. It contains no mention of V0, submitted-versus-new comparisons, discarded candidates, working variants, or the construction history of the analysis.
In concise, accessible language, it presents:

the question, including the exact preregistered hypothesis as a quotation;
what was analysed and why the chosen method addresses the question;
every deviation from the preregistration, listed explicitly;
the result in prose, figures, and digestible tables;
the exact model sample and uncertainty needed to interpret the result;
a restrained interpretation and the important limitations; and
how the conclusion changes under the registered scientific sensitivities.

The data-preparation sensitivity is presented as the gap-timing-unaware dataset under the definition above. Historical artifact names do not appear in reader-facing prose, headings, tables, figures, captions, legends, alt text, or visible link text.
The report also shows the model diagnostics needed to judge the analysis. It explains what the diagnostic displays or summaries indicate and states plainly whether the near-eye and chest-level models are acceptable, acceptable with specified limitations, or not acceptable. Diagnostic output without interpretation is not sufficient.
Near-eye measurements remain primary. Every hypothesis also has a clearly labelled chest-level section that recreates the primary figures and tables with chest-level data, rather than merely referring to an audit table or listing chest coefficients in prose.
Each report also assesses the REPORT-009 paired-placement display. When the same estimand was fitted separately at near eye and chest on the identical paired/common sample and comparison scale, include a near-eye-versus-chest estimate plot with an identity line, null lines, and equal axis geometry. If a scalar plot would be scientifically invalid or the approved analysis did not produce common-sample estimates, explain why and use the closest valid matched curve, contrast, coefficient, or table comparison without fitting a new model solely for display.
Reader-facing tables use gt. They are divided into conceptually coherent, legible pieces rather than continued across several pages or filled with audit-only columns. Complete numerical results remain available as linked CSV files. Figures and tables use familiar manuscript terminology, melEDI in reader-facing text, the registered site display rules, and 95% confidence intervals wherever they are estimable.
Displayed p-values follow REPORT-008 in prose, tables, figures, captions, and annotations. Raw and adjusted values are labelled separately; full precision is retained in source data and significance is decided before display rounding.
Necessary technical terms are explained on first use. Code may be folded, but each analytical section states what was done, why it was done, what the display shows, and what the result means.

title: How H03–H11 will be reviewed and rebuilt
section: Stage 4: Scientific description and provenance of the result-producing pipeline
text:
Stage 4: Scientific description and provenance of the result-producing pipeline
After the reader-facing result and its accepted artifacts are fixed, the same hypothesis task creates audit/hypotheses/Hxx/Hxx_analysis_preparation.qmd. This companion is the fourth documentation stage, but it does not refit or reinterpret the scientific result and does not introduce a new inferential gate. It explains how the accepted result was prepared and how its provenance can be checked without reintroducing V0 comparisons into the result report.
“Stage 4” is internal workflow shorthand. Neither “Stage 4” nor “Step 4” appears in the companion’s reader-facing title, prose, diagrams, captions, tables, callouts, or website navigation. The companion is written for an ordinary scientific reader, not for someone familiar with coordinator/worker roles, approvals, gates, task ownership, or migration history. Those internal mechanics and irrelevant construction variants are omitted.
The page follows REPORT-007 and the revised H02 exemplar. It explains what data and code produced the result, why each analytical operation was needed, what it contributed, and what evidence shows that it behaved as intended. In analytical order, it covers:

exact verified inputs and their identity, schema, key, content, and value checks;
model-frame and sample construction, exclusions, support, missingness, coverage, transformations, units, and temporal ordering;
exact participants, participant-days, observations or hours, sites, and relevant per-site or category samples;
model construction, central settings, estimands, contrasts, multiplicity, uncertainty, and inference;
convergence, distributional, residual, temporal, influence, and other applicable diagnostics;
registered sensitivity branches; and
the provenance of stored models, resampling results, predictions, figures, tables, diagnostics, source data, manifests, and claims.

The page names the hypothesis-specific scripts or modules in execution order and explains what each reads, why it is separate, and what it produces. Useful compact gt tables and plots show input distributions, support, missingness or coverage, and intermediate quantities. A Mermaid data-to-result diagram is used when it materially clarifies the chain. Technical concepts are explained on first use in specific but plain publication language.

Bounded rendering
An informational note states which bounded identity checks and lightweight descriptive calculations run during rendering and which quantities are read from stored outputs. It does not use warning, important, caution, or danger styling.
Rendering must not refit models, re-estimate autocorrelation, regenerate model predictions, rerun bootstraps or simulations, recompute Shapley analyses, or repeat other expensive scientific computation. Externally generated results need not be recomputed, but their producing scripts and exact output locations are identified.


Displays, source data, and website identity
Tables are readable and split into digestible pieces. Every figure has an informative caption, non-empty alt text, and exact paired source data. Axes use scientifically appropriate scales. Discrete masses such as exact zeros are shown separately when they would compress a continuous distribution, while the page states explicitly whether those observations remained in the fitted model.
The companion and notebooks/hypotheses/Hxx.qmd link to each other. The coordinator adds the companion immediately after the result in the Nature Health render list and navigation only after the source exists. The authoring QMD remains available in the website output and its copied bytes must match the authoring source exactly.
The hypothesis-specific preparation manifest records the source, website QMD copy, HTML, figures, paired source data, scripts, scientific outputs, environment identity, byte sizes, and SHA-256 checksums. It excludes the final worker inventory and any other self-reference that would make the checksum chain circular.


Structural verification and closure
Every hypothesis adds a focused structural test for reader-facing wording, informational callout semantics, reciprocal links and navigation, figure captions and alt text, gt tables, paired source data, bounded executable R chunks, source-copy identity, and manifest coverage. The shared verifier is scripts/pipeline/hypothesis_preparation_provenance_contract.R; each hypothesis extends it with its own required content and expensive function names.
The hypothesis task refreshes its preparation manifest, non-circular worker inventory, tests, and handoff after coordinator-owned website integration. This documentation closure does not reopen an accepted result unless it exposes a substantive discrepancy. The complete contract is recorded in audit/decisions/hypothesis_preparation_provenance_companions.md.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure
text:
The Light Exposure Behaviour Assessment (LEBA) asks about habitual light-related behaviours. The preregistered hypothesis was:

“H5: LEBA questionnaire factors correlate with selected personal light exposure metrics.”

This analysis tests whether four LEBA factor scores are associated with 17 personal light-exposure metrics after accounting for study site. Higher scores mean that the behaviour described by a factor was reported more often.






NoteAnswer in brief



None of the 68 primary near-eye associations remained statistically supported after false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment across the complete family, and the four planned sleep-environment cells are unfit for inference. The leading positive near-eye estimates remained descriptive, the complementary chest analysis reached the same family-wide conclusion, and the planned sensitivity analyses did not change that interpretation. Important model-check and site-influence limitations are summarized below.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure
text:
What was analysed
Near-eye measurements are primary because they more closely represent light near the eyes. All available chest measurements are analysed separately as complementary evidence. A common-sample analysis then fits near-eye and chest models to the same participants and participant-days, so placement differences are not confused with differences in who contributed data. The placements are never pooled as independent observations.
A predefined sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. The term means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment; it does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored. For this contrast only, the approved primary preparation could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset, because it uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant to the metric. Below, it is called simply the primary dataset.



Table 1: The four analysed LEBA factors and their score interpretation.

Interpretation

F2 includes one reverse-coded item; F3–F5 are sums of their ordered items. Every factor score was complete. Within each exact model sample, the score was centred and expressed both per raw point and per participant-level standard deviation. The report uses the latter so estimates can be compared across the four differently ranged factor scores.
Deviations and operational clarifications
The preregistration gives the broad model Metric ~ LEBA + (1|Site) but does not fully define the repeated-measure structure, response families, metric set, multiplicity family, clock handling, or placement roles. The following choices make those elements explicit.



Table 2: H05 model and inferential deviations or operational clarifications.

The fixed-site structure was more reliably estimable with nine sites.

Daily information is retained without treating days from one person as independent.

The outcome scale and support differ across the 17 metrics.

Inference and multiplicity

Table 3: H05 metric, clock, placement, and descriptive-output clarifications.













Preregistered or unspecified
Analysed
Why it matters



Metric set
Selected metrics not enumerated
Seventeen prespecified metrics, including corrected dose and MDER as the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios; both channels must be finite and positive, and at least 720 of the complete 1,440 local wall-clock minutes must be viable
The 17 × 4 cross-product fixes the 68 tests before inference.


Primary placement
Not specified in H5
All-available near eye primary; all-available chest complementary; common-sample placements as sensitivity
Separates the scientific measurement role from sample composition.


Clock outcomes
Not operationally specified
Continuous supported ranges; darkest-10-hour midpoint values strictly after 16:00 are shifted to the preceding clock scale
Avoids averaging across an artificial midnight discontinuity.


Numerical zeros in darkest-10-hour mean melEDI
Not operationally specified
A geometric-mean back-transformation residual within the unit-aware floating-point tolerance is set to exact zero only when every finite source minute in the selected window is exactly zero; missing minutes remain missing
Preserves the non-negative measurement domain without treating missing observations as zeros.


Longest period
No identifiability rule stated
All-available value treated as an observed lower bound; an exactly identified period is a sensitivity
Gaps cannot be mistaken for a continuously observed period.


Participant correlations
Correlation matrices requested
Spearman coefficients and intervals are descriptive only, without a second significance screen
The site-adjusted model family remains the inferential analysis.









For MDER, duplicated local minutes on a daylight-saving fall-back day are averaged channel by channel before their ratio is formed; absent spring-forward minutes remain missing. The daily value gives each viable minute ratio equal weight. It is not a ratio of daily integrals, and the MDER support rule changes only MDER availability rather than deleting the day from other metric analyses.
For darkest-10-hour mean melEDI, this numerical-zero rule changed three primary near-eye and five primary chest participant-days from approximately 4.16 × 10-17 lx to exactly 0 lx. It did not change a fitted sample. Only the corresponding primary L10 models, diagnostics, influence checks, paired/common primary comparison, and the mathematically dependent complete BH families were refreshed. Coefficients changed by at most 3.61 × 10-12 per LEBA point; two adjusted p-values changed below the report’s three-decimal display precision, no family rank changed, and all three families still retained zero of 68 associations. The gap-timing-unaware L10 values were already exact zeros and were not refitted.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure
text:
Models
For participant-day outcomes, the full model asks whether LEBA improves the site-adjusted description while accounting for repeated days from the same participant. The reduced model removes only LEBA. Interdaily stability (IS) and intradaily variability (IV) have one response per participant, so they do not use a participant random intercept. Fixed site effects use the registered site order and sum-to-zero contrasts; the LEBA coefficient is therefore adjusted for site without being tied to one reference site.
The following evaluated cell reads and prints the exact formula objects used for the full, reduced, and registered random-site sensitivity models.

registered_formula <- function(analysis_unit, formula_id) {
  row <- formula_registry |>
    dplyr::filter(
      .data$analysis_unit == .env$analysis_unit,
      .data$formula_id == .env$formula_id
    )
  stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1L)
  stats::as.formula(row$formula[[1L]])
}

h05_formulas <- list(
  participant_day_full = registered_formula("participant_day", "fixed_full"),
  participant_day_reduced = registered_formula("participant_day", "fixed_reduced"),
  participant_full = registered_formula("participant", "fixed_full"),
  participant_reduced = registered_formula("participant", "fixed_reduced"),
  participant_day_random_site = registered_formula("participant_day", "random_site"),
  participant_random_site = registered_formula("participant", "random_site")
)

tibble::tibble(
  Model = c(
    "Participant-day primary full",
    "Participant-day primary reduced",
    "Participant primary full",
    "Participant primary reduced",
    "Participant-day random-site sensitivity",
    "Participant random-site sensitivity"
  ),
  `Exact Wilkinson formula` = paste0(
    "`",
    vapply(h05_formulas, deparse1, character(1)),
    "`"
  )
) |>
  gt::gt(rowname_col = "Model") |>
  gt::fmt_markdown(columns = `Exact Wilkinson formula`) |>
  gt::cols_width(`Exact Wilkinson formula` ~ gt::pct(67)) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "The table is evaluated directly from the registered formula objects;",
      "the reduced model removes only LEBA from the corresponding full model."
    )
  ) |>
  h05_gt(12)

melEDI dose increased by a factor of 1.278 (95% CI 1.079–1.514), raw p = 0.004, FDR-adjusted p = 0.124.

These estimates remain useful for describing magnitude and uncertainty, but neither is a multiplicity-retained result.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure
text:
Sensitivity analyses
The common-sample placement comparison showed broad directional concordance without testing equivalence or a direct placement effect. Fixed study-site adjustment remained the primary specification because the registered random-site alternative included unstable fits. Leave-one-site-out, gap-timing-unaware, and exact-period analyses supported the same restrained family-wide interpretation while showing that some small estimates were site-sensitive.

Show detailed sensitivity results
Common near-eye and chest sample
Every plotted point compares the same metric, factor, response definition, model, transformation, and exact sample at both placements. Participant-day metrics used 107–112 participants and 489–643 matched participant-days at eight sites; IS and IV used the same 112 participant rows at eight sites. Fifty-nine of 68 associations had the same direction at both placements and overlapping component intervals; nine differed in direction but still had overlapping component intervals. Because no participant-cluster interval was calculated for the direct chest-minus-near-eye difference, these are component comparisons rather than formal tests of placement differences.







Figure 7: Exact common-sample model-scale effects, with near eye on x and chest on y. The dashed identity line describes concordance, grey lines mark the null, and equal x/y geometry preserves the 45-degree comparison. Samples contain 107–112 participants, 489–643 matched participant-days, and eight sites; IS and IV use 112 participant rows. Component 95% confidence intervals are in the adjacent tables. This is not an equivalence analysis.

Site adjustment and site influence
Fixed site was selected as primary because the inherited 17-metric site-structure evaluation fitted all fixed-site models successfully, whereas the corresponding random-site descriptions included two unstable, two non-estimable, and two singular fits. In the H05 sensitivity itself, 15 of 136 main all-available random-site fits were unstable: seven near eye and eight chest, while 121 passed. This instability is why random site is a sensitivity rather than the primary adjustment.

Gap-timing-unaware dataset
The same model implementation was applied to the gap-timing-unaware dataset, including the same mean-of-viable-momentary-ratios MDER definition. This sensitivity gave no multiplicity-retained association; its smallest value was FDR-adjusted p = 0.070. Sixty-four of 68 estimates retained their sign and had overlapping component intervals; four changed sign, also with overlapping component intervals. The conclusion that zero associations retained FDR-adjusted support is unchanged. For MDER specifically, 687 near-eye days from 137 participants entered the near-eye sensitivity family, and its smallest MDER value was FDR-adjusted p = 0.107. The matched placement sensitivity used 478 days from 107 participants at eight sites; all four directions agreed and component intervals overlapped.
Exactly identified longest period
The all-available longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI is an observed lower bound because a data gap can interrupt identifiability. The strict sensitivity retained only participant-days whose longest period was exactly identified: 500 participant-days from 132 participants at all nine sites. All four factor directions agreed with the all-available analysis.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure
text:
Interpretation
The strongest defensible conclusion is that, after fixed-site adjustment and one complete 68-test Benjamini–Hochberg correction, these data provide no multiplicity-retained evidence that any of the four LEBA factors is associated with the 17 selected personal light-exposure metrics.
The positive F2 estimates for time above 1,000 lx melEDI and melEDI dose are consistent across the principal stability checks. Their confidence intervals describe non-zero associations before multiplicity adjustment, but their adjusted values do not support confirmatory claims. They should be treated as descriptive patterns that may motivate future work, not as established effects of spending time outdoors.
This is an observational association analysis. LEBA scores are self-reported, site adjustment cannot remove all person-level confounding, only nine sites contribute to the primary analysis, and several small estimates are sensitive to site omission. Near-eye and chest measurements also represent related but non-identical light fields. Finally, the sleep-environment Tweedie models are unfit for inference because of material response-support and simulated-residual failures; their estimates and p-values are suppressed from the reader-facing results and cannot support a claim in H05. This judgment is specific to the response variable and model structure used here and does not preclude analysing the metric in another hypothesis with a different response or model.

title: How each hypothesis will be compared
H02: Daily melEDI patterns across sites and people
section: Direct comparison of near-eye and chest patterns
text:
Direct comparison of near-eye and chest patterns
The comparison used the same 112 participants, 643 participant-days, and 29,786 30-minute observations at both sensor positions across eight sites; their observation keys match one-to-one. This is the matched sample. The two positions were fitted separately with the same response definition, transformation, temporal grid, and model structure; they were not pooled.
A scalar near-eye-versus-chest identity plot would discard the feature H02 is designed to estimate: how the fitted pattern changes across the day. The figure therefore overlays the two fitted site curves at every matched half-hour. It uses only stored placement-matched predictions and does not fit a new model. The y-axis is evenly spaced on the modelling scale, with tick labels back-transformed to melEDI for interpretation.







Figure 3: Near-eye and chest site curves for the same 112 participants, 643 participant-days, and 29,786 30-minute observations at both sensor positions. Ribbons are component pointwise 95% CIs.




The ribbons are component pointwise 95% CIs for each separately fitted placement curve. They are not an interval for the near-eye-minus-chest difference because the covariance between the two fitted models was not estimated. Similar-looking curves indicate descriptive concordance on this matched sample, not statistical equivalence.

title: H05 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
NoteAbout this analysis record



This page explains how verified light-exposure metrics and questionnaire scores were turned into the H05 results. Rendering it recalculates only file-identity, schema, and key checks plus lightweight descriptive summaries from the stored H05 model frames. It reads fitted models, estimates, intervals, model checks, influence screens, and predefined alternative analyses from their recorded files. It does not fit or refit a model, calculate predictions, repeat model checks, rerun leave-one-site-out analyses, bootstrap, or simulate data.


H05 asks whether four Light Exposure Behaviour Assessment (LEBA) questionnaire factors are associated with 17 personal light-exposure metrics. The primary analysis uses the near-eye sensor position, which measures light close to the eyes. All-available chest measurements provide complementary evidence but are not interpreted as ocular exposure. A participant-day is one eligible local calendar day from one participant; participant-day metrics can therefore include repeated days from the same person.
Factor effects are reported per one participant-level standard deviation (SD) of the score, with a 95% confidence interval (95% CI). Each inferential placement or dataset applies false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment to the complete family of four factors × 17 metrics = 68 tests. Participant-level and participant-day metrics use different model structures but share the same fixed-site adjustment, which estimates one adjustment coefficient for each study site, as well as the same questionnaire-score scaling and family definition.
This page identifies the data and code that produced those results, explains why each analytical operation was necessary, and shows the stored evidence used to check the analysis. Read it alongside the H05 results report; the exact H05 linked registration-record summary is mapped there once.

title: H05 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
2. Metric construction and analytical samples
Coverage, gaps, and metric support
The primary dataset applied the general requirement of at least 50% valid minutes per hour and at least 80% valid hours per day, together with metric-specific support rules where the timing of remaining gaps affects what the metric can represent. Unsupported values remained missing rather than being interpreted as darkness. Light-level metrics use melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) in reader-facing labels, with a 0.1 lx offset where a logarithmic transform requires it. A Tweedie model is a positive-response regression model used here for non-negative, right-skewed durations while retaining exact zeros.
A sensitivity analysis repeats the accepted comparison under a predefined alternative to assess whether the interpretation is stable. One predefined sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules, but the timing of the remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For contrast at this first explanation, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset. Hereafter it is called simply the primary dataset.
MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios. Both channels must be finite and strictly positive, and at least 720 of the complete 1,440 local wall-clock minutes must provide a viable ratio. Repeated local minutes at daylight-saving fall-back are averaged channel-wise before forming the ratio; absent spring-forward minutes remain missing. Each viable minute ratio has equal weight: there is no time-profile weighting, gating, or scaling, and the daily value is not a ratio of daily integrals. Failure of this support rule makes only MDER missing; it does not delete the day from other metric analyses.
The longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI is an observed lower bound when a gap can interrupt the period. Its exact-identifiability sensitivity therefore retains only participant-days for which the longest period is fully observed. The L10 midpoint retains its continuous range and its strict-after-16:00 representation; no noon sensitivity was needed.
The shared derivation rules are documented in Preparation 04, and the model-ready datasets are documented in Preparation 06.

4. Model construction and inference
Exact formulas supplied to the models
The analysis uses fixed site with sum-to-zero contrasts as the primary site adjustment. Participant-day models add a participant random intercept because several days can come from the same participant. Participant-level IS and IV models contain one row per person and therefore do not add that intercept.

Across the H05 random-site sensitivity itself, 121 of 136 fits passed the descriptive stability checks and 15 were unstable. This is consistent with using fixed site for primary inference and random site only as a stability assessment.
Estimand, uncertainty, and multiplicity
For each metric and factor, the full model adds the centered LEBA score to the reduced site-adjusted model. The raw inferential p-value comes from that full-versus-reduced likelihood-ratio comparison. Each declared family contains all 17 metrics × 4 factors = 68 tests, and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment is performed on the complete 68-value vector. Significance is decided at adjusted p ≤ 0.05 before any display formatting.
Coefficients are converted to the metric’s practical scale and reported per one participant-level LEBA standard deviation. Gaussian identity outcomes are differences, log-transformed light outcomes are ratios, and IS is an odds ratio. Every reported interval is a two-sided 95% Wald interval from the final model. No secondary significance screen is attached to descriptive sensitivities.

NoteWhy a less conservative adjustment can accompany fewer retained associations



For one unchanged vector of raw p-values, Benjamini–Hochberg cannot retain fewer associations than Bonferroni at the same 0.05 threshold. The H05 family above is based on likelihood-ratio p-values from the fixed-site models. It is therefore not interchangeable with a family built from unadjusted rank correlations or another raw test. Multiplicity adjustment and the construction of the raw p-values are separate analytical decisions; the latter can change which associations enter the smallest ranks before either correction is applied.

5. Diagnostics and influence
Diagnostic sequence
Every stored final model was checked for convergence, Hessian status, singularity, residual behaviour, response bounds, metric-specific timing support, and within-participant serial dependence where applicable. Gaussian models use transformed-residual and influence checks. Tweedie models add simulation-based uniformity, dispersion, zero-support, and outlier checks. Candidate influential participants were ranked by Cook’s distance for ordinary linear models or by maximum absolute Pearson residual for mixed models; this screen did not silently remove observations.

Numerical-zero normalization for darkest-10-hour mean melEDI
The shared numerical-zero decision sets a geometric-mean back-transformation residual to exact zero only when it lies within the unit-aware floating-point tolerance and every finite source minute entering the selected window is exactly zero. The current sample contains 702 near-eye participant-days from 137 participants at nine sites and 732 chest participant-days from 152 participants at eight sites. One near-eye and three chest days exceeded the outer fence. All 44 day- and participant-deletion refits passed, and every chest sensitivity interval contained zero. No observation was removed from the primary analysis.
The repaired gap-timing-unaware samples contain 687 near-eye participant-days from 137 participants and 723 chest participant-days from 152 participants. The paired/common comparison contains 478 days from 107 participants at eight sites, with all four directions concordant and all component intervals overlapping. One near-eye and three chest days exceeded the outer fence. All 44 gap deletion refits passed and 40 intervals contained zero. The near-eye coefficients changed by at most 0.233 full-model standard errors without a sign reversal; the small chest F2 coefficient reversed direction in two deletions, and every chest interval contained zero. The repaired H05-F3 family still retained zero of 68 associations after BH correction.
The upper-tail summary, influence-refit record, and bounded reconciliation retain the exact inputs, samples, estimates, and preservation evidence. All 20 reconciliation checks pass; the other 16 metrics remain frozen, except for permitted complete-family BH ranks and adjusted p-values derived after the four MDER raw p-values were replaced.
The repaired sensitivity has a separate gap influence record, paired/common comparison, and 16-check reseal reconciliation. The reconciliation records 27 non-MDER adjusted-p changes and 26 rank changes caused solely by replacing the four MDER slots in H05-F3; every non-MDER raw test and fitted object is unchanged.






NoteSleep-environment outcome: unfit for H05 inference



The four primary near-eye models for time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep are unfit for H05 inference. The observed response contains exact zeros, while the fitted Tweedie simulations generated none; simulation-based uniformity and outlier checks also showed material failure, and fitted values crossed the admissible response support. Their coefficients, intervals, and p-values are therefore suppressed from the H05 results. The complementary chest models show the same material response-support and simulated-residual limitations and are also not used as inferential evidence.
This disposition is specific to this outcome as the H05 response under this model structure. It does not mean that the sleep-environment metric cannot be analysed in another hypothesis that uses a different response variable, estimand, or model structure.

Complete stored sensitivity records are available for the paired/common placement comparison, random-site analysis, leave-one-site-out analysis, gap-timing-unaware analysis, gap-timing-unaware matched MDER placement comparison, and exactly identified longest-period analysis.

title: Preparation 06: Build model-ready datasets
text:
Preparation 06 turns the checked light-exposure metrics from Preparation 04 and the fixed participant, questionnaire, and diary files acquired in Preparation 05 into inputs that hypothesis analyses can use. It first makes participant files structurally consistent, then adds participant and site context to the metric files, preserves the distinction between local clock time and actual elapsed time, and finally stores a separate input when a hypothesis method has been approved. H01 is the first such build. This step does not fit a statistical model.
The predefined gap-timing-unaware dataset still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. Its name means that the timing of remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For contrast, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a “time-sensitive primary metric dataset.” From this point onward, this report calls it simply the primary dataset.
The exact stored inputs are the current light-metric files, the fixed questionnaire and diary files, site and daylight context, elapsed-time records, and the separately prepared gap-timing-unaware dataset. Their file identities, producing scripts, and verification records are collected in the technical provenance section after the scientific sample consequences.

title: Preparation 06: Build model-ready datasets
section: 4. Preserve time of day and actual elapsed time
text:
4. Preserve time of day and actual elapsed time
Local clock time and elapsed time answer different questions. A 30-minute row labelled 08:00 represents 08:00 at every study site, which is useful for time-of-day comparisons. UTC records how much real time separated two rows, which is necessary for continuity and autocorrelation. A separate temporal-sequence operation preserves both coordinates without changing melEDI values.
When clocks move back, a local-clock interval may represent two real intervals; its stored local-clock outcome is their average. When clocks move forward, a local-clock interval can have no corresponding real interval. Only an unambiguous, usable real interval can continue an elapsed-time sequence. A real gap, unusable outcome, repeated autumn interval, or structural spring gap starts or interrupts a sequence.

Current MDER in the shared inputs
The shared inputs use the current metric version. In these files, daily MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios on a complete 1,440-position local wall-clock grid. Both channels must be finite and strictly greater than zero; a zero-denominator ratio is undefined, and a zero in either channel does not define the positive proportional comparison used by this estimand. When the autumn clock change produces duplicate local minutes, the two channels are averaged separately within that clock minute before the ratio is formed. An absent spring-forward minute remains missing.
At least 720 viable ratios are required, and exactly 720 passes the inclusive 50% rule. Failing that rule makes MDER alone unavailable: the participant-day, its other metrics, and its attached participant and site context remain in the shared inputs. Current MDER uses no time-profile weighting, exclusion, or scaling and is not a ratio of daily integrals. The older ratio-of-integrals and profile-based exclusion records document an earlier method and are not active.

In the primary dataset, MDER is available for 702 of 816 near-eye participant-days from 137 participants (mean 0.7239; median 0.7239) and 732 of 902 chest participant-days from 152 participants (mean 0.7565; median 0.7494). In the gap-timing-unaware dataset, the same momentary-ratio estimand is available for 687 of 811 near-eye participant-days from 137 participants (mean 0.7243; median 0.7239) and 723 of 897 chest participant-days from 152 participants (mean 0.7567; median 0.7495).
The stored comparison found all 25,620 non-MDER participant-day cells exactly unchanged and retained all 618 × 47 site/daylight context values exactly. Thus no non-MDER or site-context scientific value changed.
Source-verified L10 zeros in the shared inputs
L10 is the mean melEDI during the darkest 10-hour window of a participant-day. Its geometric mean can represent true zeros because production adds 0.1 lx, averages log10(melEDI + 0.1), transforms back, and subtracts 0.1 lx. In exact arithmetic, an all-zero source window therefore returns zero. Floating-point arithmetic left eight primary L10 means at 4.163336342344337e-17 lx instead. This remainder is far below the source-verified tolerance of 2.220446049250313e-14 lx.
The active numerical-zero rule stores a positive remainder within that tolerance as exact zero only when every finite source minute is exactly zero. Missing minutes remain missing; they are counted separately and are never imputed as zeros. A small positive remainder is retained if any finite source minute is positive, and a materially negative result stops production.

For an analysis that permits zero outcomes, these participant-days remain as zeros. In a two-part analysis, they remain in the zero/occurrence component and are excluded only from the strictly positive magnitude component by that component’s definition.

1. Derive the current metric layerScript: scripts/pipeline/build_metric_derivation.RModule: scripts/pipeline/metric_derivation.R; scripts/pipeline/time_support.R

Reads the eligible one-minute records and reconstructs the current metric layer. For MDER, it uses the complete 1,440-position local-clock grid, averages fall-back duplicates channel-wise, averages viable positive finite one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios, and requires at least 720 ratios. For offset geometric means, it preserves the raw back-transform and applies the source-verified METRIC-011 numerical-zero rule before storing a non-negative value. This upstream step is shown because its current manifest is an exact input to the shared model data.Stored output: artifacts/05_metrics/ and artifacts/12_manifests/metric_artifacts.csv

Reads stored one-minute inputs and the metric version identified in its verification summary; independently checks the local-clock grid, viable-pair count, MDER value, and failure reason. The stored METRIC-010 audit is tied to preceding metric manifest 7bb2830c…f43; METRIC-011 separately verified that MDER did not change in the current metric layer.Stored output: artifacts/08_diagnostics/mder_METRIC-010/verification_summary.csv

Reads the pinned one-minute gap-timing-unaware inputs and reconstructed daily outputs; independently records viable-minute support, corrected MDER availability and values, exact preservation of 25,620 non-MDER cells, and all input/output hashes. These scripts produced stored repair evidence and are not run by this report.Stored output: audit/reconciliation/mder_METRIC-010_gap_repair/ and its gap_repair_evidence_manifest.csv




7. Add site and daylight contextScript: scripts/pipeline/build_site_solar_context.RModule: scripts/pipeline/site_solar_context.R

Reads site coordinates, time zones, and all dates needed by both datasets; creates civil dawn, civil dusk, photoperiod, and descriptive solar-noon fields. Kept separate so every site/date join can be checked once.Stored output: artifacts/06_model_data/context/




8. Preserve elapsed-time provenanceScript: scripts/pipeline/build_temporal_sequence_provenance.RModule: scripts/pipeline/temporal_sequence_provenance.R

Reads accepted coverage and metric time series; links local-clock outcomes to their true UTC intervals and marks continuous elapsed-time sequences. Kept separate because time-of-day and elapsed-time questions require different coordinates.Stored output: artifacts/06_model_data/temporal_provenance/




9. Create shared model inputsScript: scripts/pipeline/build_base_model_data.RModule: scripts/pipeline/base_model_data.R

Reads the current metric manifest, standardized participant inputs, and site context; attaches one matching context record while retaining metric rows and recording participant-input availability. The base manifest pins the current METRIC-011 metric manifest and input bundle. Kept separate from hypothesis-specific exclusions.Stored output: artifacts/06_model_data/base/




10. Store H01 primary framesScript: scripts/pipeline/build_h01_model_data.RModule: scripts/pipeline/h01_model_data.R

Reads the shared model inputs and approved H01 metric contract; stores outcomes, predictors, metric-specific inclusion records, and sample flow for 17 metrics. No model is fitted.Stored output: artifacts/06_model_data/H01.rds and artifacts/06_model_data/H01/




11. Store gap-timing-unaware H01 framesScript: scripts/pipeline/build_h01_manuscript_prepared_data.RModule: scripts/pipeline/h01_manuscript_prepared_adapter.R

Reads the gap-timing-unaware data and applies the same H01 implementation contract. Kept separate so shared model code can be checked without erasing the preparation difference.Stored output: artifacts/06_model_data/H01/scenarios/manuscript_prepared_data/




12. Store pre-analysis displaysScript: scripts/pipeline/build_preanalysis_comparison.RModule: scripts/pipeline/preanalysis_comparison.R

Reads both stored preparations; writes descriptive count, distribution, reconciliation, and figure-source records before hypothesis fitting. It does not test a scientific hypothesis.Stored output: artifacts/08_diagnostics/preanalysis_comparison/




13. Record the preceding MDER repin and invarianceScript: audit/scripts/rebuild_mder_METRIC_010_downstream.RModule: Preceding downstream repin and invariance record

Records the METRIC-010 manifest identities after the repaired gap-timing-unaware input moved through site context, shared inputs, H01 preparations, and the descriptive comparison. It verifies that all 618 by 47 site-context values were exact. METRIC-011 supersedes those identities but not this version-specific invariance record.Stored output: artifacts/08_diagnostics/mder_METRIC-010/downstream_rebuild/ and its rebuild_manifest.csv




14. Verify and reseal numerical-zero normalizationScript: audit/scripts/finalize_l10_METRIC_011.RModule: scripts/pipeline/verify_metric_derivation_core.R; scripts/pipeline/verify_metric_derivation_mder.R

Reads the rebuilt primary metric layer, its preserved pre-repair snapshot, and the exact L10 source windows. It verifies the numerical-zero decisions and current metric layer, proves that only eight primary L10 means changed, confirms that the gap-timing-unaware scientific values did not change, and reseals dependent preparation manifests. No hypothesis model is fitted or refitted.Stored output: audit/reconciliation/l10_METRIC-011/ and its METRIC-011_evidence_manifest.csv




Paths identify the external production code and accepted outputs; the render does not source these files.

title: Descriptive tables and figures
text:
The primary analytical measurement is near eye melEDI. Chest measurement is shown as a complementary description; values from the two placements are never pooled and are not treated as equivalent.
The study sites are displayed in the registered reader order, with country codes and fixed colours: Borås (SE), Delft (NL), Dortmund (DE), Tübingen (DE), Munich (DE), Madrid (ES), Izmir (TR), San José (CR), Kumasi (GH). The same labels, order, and colours are used throughout the tables and figures.
The normalized participant roster contains 191 participants. After the pre-specified ≥80% full-day completeness rule and exact-all-zero screen, the primary near eye dataset contains 141 participants, 816 participant-days, and 1,175,160 one-minute real observations. The complementary chest dataset contains 154 participants, 902 participant-days, and 1,298,880 one-minute real observations. The paired subset contains 112 participants and 643 participant-days.

title: Descriptive tables and figures
text:
This document reproduces the submitted table styles, figure compositions, and manuscript-scale canvases from the earlier manuscript-generating descriptive analysis, but fills them with the updated verified data. It also repairs errors that could not responsibly be copied forward. The main analytical measurement is near-eye melEDI; chest measurement is shown only as a complementary description and the two placements are never pooled.
The replicated layouts include the wide participant-and-site table, the wide site-by-metric table with miniature distributions, the five-part study overview, the 3 × 3 site profiles, the 4 × 4 metric grid, the four-panel time-series explanation, the latitude–photoperiod diagnostic, and the site-by-state light-context table.
All 13 required shared manifests matched their pinned SHA-256 fingerprints before any analytical input was read. The current display registry is config/site_display_registry.csv; it supplies the labels, visible order, and colours in every table and figure. The visible site sequence is Borås (SE), Delft (NL), Dortmund (DE), Tübingen (DE), Munich (DE), Madrid (ES), Izmir (TR), San José (CR), Kumasi (GH).

title: Descriptive tables and figures
text:
Table 2: metric distributions
Table 4 reproduces the old metric categories, order, ten site columns, scaling column, and enlarged miniature distribution column. Every numerical cell states N, the number of participants, and d, the number of participant-days with a finite value. The site columns have equal widths and each median, interval, mean ± SD, and size line is kept intact. A compact line under each metric name states what the metric captures and why that construct is physiologically or health-relevant; these notes are context, not health- effect estimates from this descriptive dataset.
MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI / photopic illuminance ratios, with both channels finite and strictly positive. Each day is evaluated on a complete 1,440-minute local wall-clock grid and retained with at least 720 viable ratios (the inclusive 50% rule). Fall-back duplicate local minutes are averaged within channel before the ratio is formed; spring-forward absent minutes remain missing.
For the L10 mean, source windows verified as entirely zero are retained as exact 0 lx. Machine-precision residuals from the averaging calculation are not interpreted as positive exposure.
