title: Descriptive tables and figures
text:
Figure 1: study overview
The study overview retains the submitted five-part composition: protocol, site map, collection timing, photoperiod coverage, and a repeated 48-hour near-eye profile. The second 24-hour cycle is a display duplicate, not additional data. Collection spans are shown as rectangles and split only when a site has at least six consecutive dates without any available data.







Figure 1: Study protocol, locations, collection dates, observed civil photoperiod, and the pooled main near-eye 48-hour double profile.




Panel B restores the submitted country and coordinate information while retaining the registered site names and colours. The black and site-coloured profiles use LightLogR::aggregate_Datetime() in 15-minute floor bins after removing participant grouping; the numeric handler is the median with na.rm = TRUE. Nested grey ribbons show the central 50% and 90% of eligible one-minute values in each overall bin, with direct arrow labels. They are value intervals, not confidence intervals. The red band from the lower plot edge to −0.1 shows average diary sleep and the blue shading shows average civil night; declared non-wear is not displayed. The melEDI axis uses LightLogR::symlog_trans(base = 10, thr = 1, scale = 1) and is capped above 10,000 lx to reserve less space for unsupported extremes.

title: Descriptive tables and figures
text:
Figure 2: site-specific profiles
The main near-eye profiles retain the earlier 3 × 3 double-plot layout and registered site order. Each site uses the same 15-minute aggregate_Datetime() median with nested central 50%, 75%, and 95% value intervals. The interval legend shows the corresponding ribbon opacities. The red mean-sleep strip extends from the lower plot edge to −0.1. The taller, 450-dpi exports preserve the accepted visual grammar while improving detail.







Figure 2: Pooled main near-eye melEDI profiles by site, with each 24-hour cycle repeated once.

title: H01: Site differences in personal light exposure
text:
The preregistered H1 hypothesis was:

“Personal light-exposure metrics differ across sites after accounting for latitude and photoperiod.”

The scientific question is whether the 17 personal-light-exposure metrics show site, photoperiod, or latitude associations across the international study sites. Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) is an illuminance weighted for melanopsin-related sensitivity. The near-eye sensor position is primary because it samples light closer to the eyes during wear, but it does not directly measure retinal exposure. The chest sensor position provides complementary evidence about light measured at the chest, not ocular exposure, and is not pooled with near-eye measurements.
The analysis treats site and latitude as separate explanations. Each site has one latitude, so a fixed-site model and a linear-latitude model cannot be interpreted as independent covariates in one ordinary fixed-effects model. Instead, both models use the same observations and photoperiod adjustment, and their adequacy is compared on that common frame.






NoteAnswer in brief



After false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment in four separate complete 17-test families, the primary near-eye analysis supported 10 metrics for overall site, 12 for photoperiod, and 7 for latitude.
Per additional hour of photoperiod, consequential examples were a ×1.18 [1.11–1.26] ratio in mean melEDI, and -0.13 [-0.20–-0.07] h less calendar-day cumulative time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep; last light above 250 lx melEDI occurred 0.32 [0.19–0.46] h later, and each bracketed range is a 95% confidence interval (95% CI).
Fixed effects represented 5.9–27.8% of outcome variation across metrics, while complete models represented 5.9–61.1%.
The current MDER was supported for overall site (FDR-adjusted p <0.001), photoperiod (FDR-adjusted p <0.001), latitude (FDR-adjusted p = 0.013), and site-versus-linear-latitude adequacy (FDR-adjusted p = 0.010). MDER increased by 0.024 per additional hour of photoperiod (95% CI 0.017 to 0.031) and decreased by -0.014 per 10° absolute latitude (95% CI -0.024 to -0.004).
Complementary chest evidence retained the broad geographic pattern; among the same participants and participant-days at both sensor positions, 26 of 30 matched photoperiod or latitude estimates lay on the same side of the null, although 5 FDR-adjusted support decisions differed; relative to the primary dataset, which for this contrast can be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset, the gap-timing-unaware near-eye sensitivity still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules but did not use the timing of remaining missing observations for metric-specific adjustment; it changed 7 of 68 metric-question decisions.

title: H01: Site differences in personal light exposure
text:
What was analysed
The response package contains 17 metrics spanning temporal dynamics, level, duration, exposure history, spectrum, and timing. A participant-day is one participant contributing one retained daily record on one local calendar day under the H01 day definition. Participant-day outcomes use a participant random intercept: this random effect represents remaining between-participant variation after the reported predictors are considered. Participant-level dynamics outcomes use ordinary Gaussian models because each participant contributes one analytical observation. Each response uses its declared Gaussian transformation or Tweedie log-link family; the same implementation is used for both data scenarios.
MDER is calculated as the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI-to-illuminance ratios. A minute is viable when both channels are finite and strictly positive, and a day contributes MDER when at least 720 viable minute ratios are available.
The all-available sample uses all retained metric-specific observations at one sensor position. Across these outcomes, the primary near-eye samples used 137–141 participants and 655–816 participant-days across 9 sites. The complementary chest samples used 152–154 participants and 732–902 participant-days across 8 sites. A matched sample restricts each metric to the same participants and participant-days at the near-eye and chest positions; the positions are still fitted separately. Exact metric-specific samples are retained in the detailed analysis record.
After the first explanation above, the time-sensitive dataset is called the primary dataset and the alternative sensitivity is called the gap-timing-unaware dataset. The complete registration changes and related records are retained later in this report.
Metric derivation is documented in Preparation 04, and the model-ready rows and sample construction are documented in Preparation 06.

title: H01: Site differences in personal light exposure
text:
Statistical models
Site, photoperiod, latitude, and site-versus-linear-latitude adequacy are four separate model-level questions. Their raw p-values are adjusted as four separate complete 17-test FDR families. A site-specific follow-up is made only when the corresponding overall site test has a FDR-adjusted p < 0.050. That follow-up compares each site with the site-average estimate, an average across sites that gives each site equal weight, reports a difference or ratio with a 95% CI, and applies a within-metric FDR adjustment.
Gaussian fixed-effect comparisons use maximum likelihood; final Gaussian participant-day fits use restricted maximum likelihood. Tweedie models use a log link and maximum likelihood throughout. Gaussian responses use their declared identity, log10(value + 0.1), logit, or shifted linear-clock transformation. A back-transformed estimate returns a model-scale estimate to its displayed original or practical unit. Exact evaluated formula objects, engines, and estimation methods are retained in the technical reproducibility section.

title: H01: Site differences in personal light exposure
text:
Results in brief
In the primary near-eye analysis, the four complete correction families supported 8 metrics for overall site, 12 for photoperiod, 6 for latitude, and 8 for site-versus-linear-latitude adequacy. The complementary chest analysis supported 13, 12, 9, and 11 metrics, respectively. This is evidence that the personal light exposome varies with geography, but the metric-specific pattern is sensitive to placement and analytical sample.

Variation represented
Marginal R² is the share of variation represented by the complete set of fixed predictors. Conditional R² adds the participant random effect, and the participant-associated share is conditional minus marginal R² for participant-day models. A term-specific part-R² records the reduction in R² when that term is removed from its model. Site and photoperiod part-R² values can contain overlapping information and must not be summed; latitude part-R² belongs to the separate latitude model.

title: H01: Site differences in personal light exposure
text:
Model diagnostics
All 34 primary and complementary point fits converged with positive-definite Hessians. A model is acceptable when no reviewed diagnostic is flagged, acceptable with limitations when optimization is valid but a residual, prediction-bound, construct, or clock-scale signal requires disclosure, and not acceptable when a required fit or hard diagnostic fails. None of the 34 models is classified as not acceptable. A review signal is therefore not a convergence failure and does not by itself justify changing a response family.
The diagnostic matrix evaluates:

convergence and Hessian validity, which indicate whether the numerical optimum was obtained and locally identified;
random-effect singularity, which checks whether an estimated variance component collapsed to its boundary;
residual distribution, which detects residual-shape, dispersion, zero-mass, or outlier discrepancies;
prediction bounds, which check verified physical lower and upper limits;
the calendar-day cumulative construct audit for pre-sleep time; and
the strict-after-16:00 linearization check for clock outcomes.

title: H01: Site differences in personal light exposure
text:
Interpretation
The primary results support the hypothesis that personal light exposure differs geographically, but they do not reduce that pattern to one universal site ordering or one latitude effect. After FDR adjustment in the four separate complete 17-test families, overall site was supported for 10 of 17 metrics, photoperiod for 12, latitude for 7, and site-versus-linear-latitude adequacy for 9. The two dynamics metrics retained none of these associations. In contrast, the three level metrics retained site, photoperiod, and latitude support for 3, 3, 2 metrics, respectively; the five duration metrics retained 2, 4, 1; and the five timing metrics retained 4, 3, 3. Thus geography appeared most consistently in light level and timing, whereas duration responses were more consistently related to photoperiod.
MDER, the spectrum metric, retained support for all four model-level questions. Its positive photoperiod association and negative linear-latitude association summarize broad gradients, while the supported site-versus-linear- latitude comparison shows that a single latitude slope does not capture all represented site structure.
Among supported ratio-scale photoperiod effects, an additional hour of day length corresponded to approximately 9–28% higher responses, depending on metric. Examples include mean melEDI at ×1.18 [1.11–1.26], calendar-day cumulative pre-sleep time below 10 lx melEDI at -0.13 [-0.20–-0.07] h, and last light above 250 lx melEDI at 0.32 [0.19–0.46] h. Hierarchical site contrasts then identify which sites differ from the site-average estimate, but only for metrics with a supported overall site test; their varying directions rule out a single north-to-south site ranking.
The R² summaries distinguish complete-model variation, participant-associated variation, and term-level part R². They should not be interpreted as an additive decomposition: site and photoperiod can contain overlapping information, and latitude belongs to a separate same-frame model. Across the 17 primary metrics, fixed effects represented 5.9–27.8% and complete models represented 5.9–61.1%. For participant-day outcomes, the participant-associated share ranged from 11.0 to 39.1%. When averaged only over metrics whose corresponding model-level test was supported, term part R² was 8.7% for site (10 metrics), 5.9% for photoperiod (12 metrics), and 3.8% for latitude (7 metrics).
The complementary chest analysis reproduced the broad geographic signal, but the placement-specific all-available heatmap is not a test of placement. In the matched samples containing the same participants and participant-days at both sensor positions, 26 of 30 comparable photoperiod and latitude point estimates were on the same side of the null and 5 FDR-adjusted support decisions differed. This indicates material metric-level placement sensitivity without implying equivalence, a formal placement effect, or that one placement can substitute for the other. The gap-timing-unaware near-eye sensitivity changed 7 of 68 support decisions, so individual metric claims remain conditional on the timing-aware metric preparation even though the broad geographic conclusion persists.

title: H01: Site differences in personal light exposure
text:
Limitations

The design is observational; associations with site, photoperiod, and latitude are not causal effects.
Site and latitude are structurally linked because every site has one latitude. Separate same-frame models address estimability but cannot remove all geographic confounding.
Many models are acceptable with limitations because residual-shape or prediction-bound checks require review. The representative plots and stored model-check values make the main warning types inspectable and should temper tail-sensitive interpretation.
Near-eye and chest sensors measure related but different exposure environments. Chest measurements are complementary and must not be relabelled as ocular exposure.
Rows from the gap-timing-unaware dataset do not retain measurement-support hours, so those hours remain unavailable.
The calendar-day cumulative pre-sleep outcome can include more than one diary-defined pre-sleep interval. Values strictly above six hours are audited but are not capped.

title: Preparation 01: Import and align light, sleep, and wear data
text:
Preparation 01 establishes the measurement record that all later preparation steps use. The production workflow reads the fixed light-logger, sleep-diary, and wear-log releases from nine study sites. It checks their identities, converts the logger observations to complete one-minute values, preserves both actual and local clock time, and assigns a measurement context to each minute. Its outputs enter Preparation 02, where hourly and daily coverage is assessed.
The scientific inputs are 35 fixed local source files: light-logger, sleep-diary, and wear-log files from recorded site releases. Their exact release identities and file checks are documented in the technical sections at the end of this page.

section: 2. Preserve actual time and local clock time
text:
2. Preserve actual time and local clock time
Two time coordinates are retained because they answer different questions. datetime_utc identifies the actual instant and is used to order readings and measure elapsed time. datetime_wall represents the local clock reading, so 08:00 has the same time-of-day meaning at every site. At an autumn clock change, one local minute can correspond to two actual instants. The stored audit contains 360 such participant-level wall-clock minutes—120 for Madrid (ES) near-eye data, 120 for Madrid (ES) chest data, and 120 for Tübingen (DE) near-eye data. They remain distinct in UTC and are not discarded or averaged during import.
The original logger interval is inferred separately for each participant and placement. A one-minute value is retained only when all expected original readings in that minute are present and finite. 3. Prepare sleep and wear periods
The sleep diary defines the interval from sleep preparation to wake. Its start is included and its end is excluded. These measurements characterize the bedside sleep environment and remain part of the intended hybrid 24-hour record. The wear log supplies additional context. An off label while awake is treated as true non-wear; sleep and site_leave labels are retained for provenance but do not independently remove a light value.

section: Production scripts and why the operations are separate
text:
Production scripts and why the operations are separate
The producing code is listed in execution order in Table Table 12. Separating source identity, temporal aggregation, interval preparation, state matching, and verification leaves a stored checkpoint at each scientifically consequential boundary.



Table 12: Producing scripts and function modules in execution order; none is executed while this report renders.










Step and producing code
Reads, operation, separation, and output




1scripts/pipeline/build_import_alignment.Rscripts/pipeline/import_sources.R

Reads config/site_sources.csv, resolves each fixed repository revision and DOI, checks the local source-file fingerprint, and loads the named object. This is separate so source identity is established before any time or state transformation. Outputs: cached fixed source files plus artifacts/02_aligned/source_audit.csv.



2scripts/pipeline/time_axes.Rscripts/pipeline/aggregation_coverage.R

Reads the original logger records, preserves UTC as actual time and local clock time as wall time, infers each participant-device recording interval, and creates a one-minute value only when every expected original reading is present and finite. This is separate so temporal completeness is checked before diary or wear information can affect validity. Outputs: artifacts/01_imported/minute/ and the time and recording-interval audits.



3scripts/pipeline/state_alignment.R

Reads the fixed sleep diaries and wear logs, checks interval bounds and overlap, and stores valid half-open intervals. Unusable entries are recorded rather than silently repaired. Outputs: artifacts/02_aligned/state_intervals/, state_interval_audit.csv, and state_interval_summary.csv.



4scripts/pipeline/state_alignment.Rscripts/pipeline/state_interval_projection.R

Matches the checked intervals to one-minute light rows without changing row cardinality, derives bedside-sleep, worn, and true non-wear contexts, and applies the melEDI operating limit. Kept separate from interval preparation so matching can be audited independently. Outputs: per-site and combined files under artifacts/02_aligned/ plus state, join, saturation, and sample audits.



5scripts/pipeline/verify_import_alignment_artifacts.R

Reads the completed outputs and independently checks manifest identity, source-fingerprint propagation, unique keys, signal-validity flags, and the accepted placement totals. It does not rebuild data. Output: a pass/fail verification result; no scientific artifact is written.

title: Preparation 02: Assess coverage and document sample flow
text:
Preparation 02 evaluates whether the aligned one-minute records from Preparation 01 contain enough valid melEDI to represent an hour or a complete participant-day. It reads the stored near-eye and chest files separately, constructs a complete local-clock grid for every participant-date present in those files, and records hourly and daily coverage decisions. The accepted outputs enter Preparation 03 for reference-profile learning and Preparation 04 for metric derivation.
The primary dataset uses the full 1,440-minute hybrid measurement day, including bedside sleep-environment measurements. A day passes when at least 80% of those minutes have valid melEDI. The 50% hourly rule is applied only when an hourly summary is needed; a failed hour does not erase its observed minutes from the daily decision or from minute-based metrics.
The separately predefined gap-timing-unaware dataset still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. Its name means that the timing of remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For contrast, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a “time-sensitive primary metric dataset.” This report presents the general coverage step for the primary dataset; the separate dataset is constructed and identified later in the preparation chain.

title: Preparation 03: Learn fixed time-of-day reference profiles
text:
Preparation 03 learned fixed time-of-day reference profiles from the participant-days retained in Preparation 02. These profiles describe when melEDI and illuminance were typically observed across the day while giving each participant equal influence. Preparation 04 uses them to judge whether a participant-day was observed at the times that matter for a particular metric. The profiles do not replace an observed measurement and, except for the explicitly permitted additive dose correction, do not change a metric value.
The exact scientific inputs were:


near-eye Rule A one-minute records;

chest Rule A one-minute records;

the stored Rule A settings.

The outputs are the fixed intensity profiles, the strict-threshold timing distribution, metric-specific relevance maps, their support summaries, and the provenance records under artifacts/04_reference_profiles/. They are passed to Preparation 04.

title: Preparation 03: Learn fixed time-of-day reference profiles
text:
What the production step did
The production workflow separated time alignment, profile learning, and artifact verification so that each scientific operation had a narrow, checkable responsibility. Table 1 states the rules in the order in which they affected the data.



Table 1: Scientific decisions used to learn the fixed reference profiles.











Decision
Recorded operation
Why it is needed



Eligible input
Use the one-minute near-eye and chest files that passed Preparation 02 Rule A. The complete hybrid 24-hour day includes bedside measurements during diary-defined sleep.
The reference must represent the same eligible measurement days that enter metric derivation.


Time coordinate
Retain every observation in actual time and make a separate local-clock copy for learning 48 fixed 30-minute periods.
Actual time preserves chronology; local clock aligns observations that occurred at the same time of day.


Participant balance
Within each 30-minute period, take each participant's median and then the median across participants.
Participants with more recorded days or minutes cannot dominate the population reference.


Threshold timing
Within every participant-day and period, calculate the fraction of valid melEDI minutes strictly above 250 lx; average days within participant and then participants within profile.
A population median may remain below 250 lx even when individual days contain threshold events.


Profile variants
Store pooled, site-specific, and leave-one-site-out versions for full-day, wake, three hours before sleep, and sleep periods.
Preparation 04 can use the pooled profile and examine prespecified site-related sensitivity inputs without relearning profiles.


Insufficient support
Require 20 participants for pooled and leave-one-site-out full-day profiles and five for site- or diary-period-specific profiles. Retain unsupported periods without interpolation.
Missing support remains explicit and cannot be replaced by an invented time-of-day pattern.



These are stored production decisions. No profile-learning operation is executed during this render.








The complete full day is the intended hybrid 24-hour measurement cycle, including bedside measurements during diary-defined sleep. Wake, sleep, and the three hours before sleep are separate profile domains; they do not redefine which days passed the general coverage rule.

section: Probability of exceeding 250 lx by time of day
text:
Probability of exceeding 250 lx by time of day
The timing of strict melEDI values above 250 lx cannot be inferred from whether the population median profile itself exceeds 250 lx. Individual participant-days may cross the threshold even when the population median remains lower. Preparation 03 therefore learned a separate probability for each half-hour period:

within every participant-day, it calculated the fraction of valid minutes with melEDI strictly greater than 250 lx;
it gave days equal weight within each participant; and
it then gave participants equal weight within the pooled, site-specific, or leave-one-site-out distribution.

title: Preparation 04: Derive light-exposure metrics
text:
Preparation 04 converts the eligible one-minute light records from Preparation 02 into the daily, diary-period, 30-minute, hourly, and participant-level metrics used by later analyses. It also records whether each individual metric had enough relevant data to be interpreted. A failed support check makes only that metric unavailable; it does not discard the participant-day from unrelated analyses. For offset geometric means, it also records when floating-point roundoff is normalized to a source-verified exact zero.
The exact inputs are the Preparation 02 Rule A coverage files, the Preparation 01 sleep and wear intervals, and the fixed time-of-day profiles and relevance maps learned in Preparation 03. The main outputs are eight R data files containing participant-day, participant, 30-minute, and hourly values for the near-eye and chest placements. Preparation 06 combines those files with site and participant context; this report does not inspect any hypothesis result.

ImportantInterpret the full-day metrics as a hybrid measurement



During wake and the three hours before sleep, the record represents the logger’s worn placement: near-eye or chest. During diary-defined sleep, it represents the bedside sleep environment. A metric spanning the full day is therefore an environmental-light summary of this planned hybrid record, not a continuous 24-hour measure of ocular exposure.

NoteShort glossary





Metric support: the observed data available at the times relevant to a particular metric; insufficient support makes that metric unavailable but does not remove the participant-day.

Transformed and back-transformed quantities: calculations may be made on a scale chosen for statistical or numerical reasons; back-transformation returns the result to its original practical unit, such as lx.

title: Preparation 04: Derive light-exposure metrics
text:
Scientific rules applied during production



Table 2: Metric construction, temporal support, and missing-data rules applied by the production scripts.










Scientific operation
Rule and reason



Measurement represented
The full day is a placement-specific hybrid: near-eye or chest measurement while awake, plus bedside sleep-environment measurement during diary-defined sleep. It is not continuous 24-hour ocular exposure.


Actual time and local clock
Actual UTC time preserves order, elapsed duration, gaps, adjacency, and both repeated autumn hours. Local clock aligns time-of-day bins, M10/L10, timing, and interdaily stability.


Thirty-minute and hourly values
A 30-minute arithmetic mean needs 15 of 30 valid minutes. An hourly zero-aware geometric mean needs 30 of 60 and uses a 0.1 lx offset so true zeros remain valid. Unsupported bins stay as missing rows.


Numerical zeros after geometric means
After adding 0.1 lx, averaging on the log10 scale, and transforming back, production subtracts the offset. A result within the unit-aware floating-point tolerance is stored as exact zero only when every finite source value is exact zero; negative light beyond tolerance stops production. Missing minutes stay missing and never become zero.


Thresholds and missing minutes
Comparisons are strictly >1,000, >250, <10, and <1 lx melEDI. Missing or invalid minutes are never converted to zero or darkness and never bridge a continuous period.


Diary-period metrics
Wake, pre-sleep, and sleep values require 80% support in that specific diary period; 70% and 90% are fixed sensitivities. An incomplete diary domain, absent period, or inadequate support affects only that metric.


Dose and MDER
Observed dose integrates actual durations. Only dose may be corrected for when missing data occurred, with at least 80% profile relevance and a maximum factor of 1.25. MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios on the 1,440-position local-clock grid. Both channels must be finite and strictly positive, and at least 720 ratios are required. It is not weighted, scaled, profile-gated, or calculated as a ratio of daily integrals.


Brightest and darkest 10 hours
M10 tests all 841 non-wrapping one-minute starts; L10 tests all 1,440 starts and may cross midnight. Each window is 600 minutes, uses at least 80% ordinary and profile support, and returns a geometric mean and midpoint. The same source-verified numerical-zero rule applies to the geometric mean. No L5 metric is produced.


Timing and longest continuous period
First, last, and mean timing above 250 lx require sufficient support where such events are expected. The longest observed uninterrupted period is a lower bound; a possible upper bound and exact-only sensitivity preserve uncertainty caused by missing data.


Interdaily stability and intradaily variability
Both need at least three eligible days. Interdaily stability needs 20 clock hours represented on at least two days; intradaily variability needs 24 truly adjacent hourly pairs across at least three days.









Source-verified zeros after geometric means
Geometric means can include true zero measurements because production first adds 0.1 lx, averages on the log10 scale, transforms back, and subtracts the same 0.1 lx. In exact arithmetic, an all-zero source window returns zero. Floating-point arithmetic can instead leave a minute positive remainder: the eight affected L10 means were 4.163336342344337e-17 lx, far below the source-verified numerical tolerance of 2.220446049250313e-14 lx.
The active numerical-zero rule stores a positive remainder within that tolerance as exact zero only when every finite source minute is itself exactly zero. Missing minutes remain missing; they are counted separately and never imputed as zeros. A materially negative result stops production, and a small positive result with any positive source minute is retained.

The remaining chest window contained 547 observed zero minutes and 53 missing minutes; all 547 observed values were zero, and the 53 missing minutes stayed missing. L10 remains available for all 816 near-eye and 902 chest participant-days, so neither the sample nor its support rule changed. Every non-L10 value and all samples are unchanged. No hypothesis model is run or rebuilt by this report.
The sealed audit contains 12 numerical-zero normalizations in total: four previously documented negative roundoff residuals and the eight positive residuals above. A zero-capable analysis retains these participant-days as exact zeros; a later two-part model retains them in its zero/occurrence part and excludes them only from a strictly positive magnitude part by definition.
The central distinction is between participant-day eligibility and metric-specific availability. A day that passed the general coverage rule remains in the prepared data even when, for example, its pre-sleep period is unknown, its M10 window has insufficient support, or its paired illuminance data cannot support MDER.

The 80% column is primary. Incomplete diary domains and absent target periods remain distinct from insufficient observed melEDI support.








At the primary cutoff, the near-eye output retains 737 wake, 655 pre-sleep, and 778 sleep-environment values. The chest output retains 818, 743, and 861, respectively. An unavailable value carries one of three distinct explanations: the diary could not bound the day’s state domains, the target period did not occur, or the target period contained too little valid melEDI.
MDER from viable one-minute channel pairs
The melanopic daylight efficacy ratio (MDER) describes melEDI relative to photopic illuminance. For each participant-day, production first represents the complete 1,440-position local wall-clock grid. If the autumn clock change creates two observations for one local minute, melEDI and illuminance are each averaged within that clock minute before their ratio is formed. A local minute that does not exist during the spring clock change remains missing.
A minute contributes only when both channels are finite and strictly greater than zero. This restriction defines a viable proportional comparison: a zero illuminance denominator is undefined, and a zero in either channel does not represent a meaningful positive channel ratio for this estimand. MDER is the arithmetic mean of the viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios. At least 720 of the 1,440 positions must be viable; the boundary is inclusive, so exactly 720 passes. If fewer are viable, only MDER is unavailable. The participant-day and all other metrics remain eligible.
No time profile weights, gates, or scales enter current MDER, and it is not a ratio of daily channel integrals. Records describing a profile-supported ratio-of-integrals method and 70%, 80%, or 90% MDER gates document an earlier method; they are not active.
The gap-timing-unaware dataset still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. Its name means that the timing of remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For this first explanation only, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset; hereafter it is called simply the primary dataset. Both datasets now use the same momentary-ratio MDER definition.

title: H01 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
H01 asks whether personal light exposure differs among study sites. The analysis treats the near-eye sensor position as primary because it samples light closer to the eyes during wear, while recognizing that it does not directly measure retinal exposure. The chest sensor position provides complementary evidence about light measured at the chest, not ocular exposure. The 17-response package includes melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI), an illuminance weighted for melanopsin-related sensitivity, and distinguishes an overall site association from photoperiod and absolute latitude.
The current MDER construct is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI-to-illuminance ratios. Both channels must be finite and strictly positive, and at least 720 viable minute ratios are required for a retained participant-day MDER value.
This record explains which data and code produced those results, why each operation was needed, what it contributed, and what evidence shows that it behaved as intended. The sections follow the data-to-result sequence.
A model frame is the exact set of rows and variables used for one fitted model. Each response-specific frame is fixed before that model is fitted.
The H01 results report presents the scientific findings and its linked registration-record summary. Model estimates and 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs), model checks, influence results, and joint-refit summaries are read from stored outputs. This page does not fit or compare models, regenerate predictions, or repeat resampling.
False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment is applied separately to each of four complete 17-test families. A participant-day is one participant contributing one retained daily record on one local calendar day under the H01 day definition. Where a site-average estimate is reported, it is an average across sites that gives each site equal weight.

1. Data entering the analysis
Verified inputs
Two prepared datasets enter the analysis. The primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset because the timing of remaining missing observations is used where it matters for the metric. Each H01 analysis dataset contains the 17-metric contract, long model rows, sample flow, exclusions, predictor centres, scenario availability, a variable dictionary, and input provenance. Eight analysis scenarios
The same implementation creates two placements × two prepared datasets × two sample definitions. The all-available near-eye primary dataset is the primary analysis. Chest is fitted separately. title: H01 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
4. Model construction
Exact formula set
The implementation uses ordinary Gaussian linear models for participant-level outcomes and Gaussian linear mixed models or Tweedie generalized mixed models for participant-day outcomes. Participant-day models include a participant random intercept, representing remaining between-participant variation after the reported predictors are considered. Site and latitude models are fitted separately so that a nine-level site factor is never interpreted as a single latitude coefficient.

Show the R code used for this displayformula_manifest |>
  distinct(.data$analysis_unit, .data$model_name, .data$formula) |>
  mutate(
    `Model unit` = recode(
      .data$analysis_unit,
      participant = "Participant",
      participant_day = "Participant-day"
    ),
    Model = str_to_sentence(str_replace_all(.data$model_name, "_", " ")),
    Formula = paste0("`", str_squish(.data$formula), "`")
  ) |>
  select(.data$`Model unit`, .data$Model, .data$Formula) |>
  gt::gt(groupname_col = "Model unit") |>
  gt::fmt_markdown(columns = "Formula") |>
  gt::cols_width(Model ~ gt::pct(22), Formula ~ gt::pct(78)) |>

The complete site model estimates site and photoperiod jointly. The reduced site model removes site; the reduced photoperiod model removes photoperiod. The latitude model substitutes centred absolute latitude, expressed per 10°, for the site factor while retaining the same photoperiod term. All comparison fits use maximum likelihood; final Gaussian mixed models are refitted with restricted maximum likelihood for coefficient and variance reporting.

Marginal R² is the variation represented by all fixed predictors. Conditional R² adds the participant random effect, and the participant-associated share is their difference for participant-day models. Term-specific part-R² records the reduction when one term is removed from its model. These term-specific contributions can overlap and must not be summed; latitude belongs to a separate same-frame model.
The four model-level questions form four separate complete 17-test FDR families. The Benjamini–Hochberg method is applied separately within each family and never only to metrics that happened to have small raw p-values.

section: 10. How to examine or reproduce H01
text:
10. How to examine or reproduce H01
A reader can inspect the chain in four passes:

compare h01_contract.R with the two pinned model-data manifests to confirm the 17 responses, eight runs, transformations, and formulas;
compare the sample and retention displays above with model_rows.csv, sample_flow.csv, and H01_exact_samples_by_site.csv;
follow the producing script and SHA-256 identity in each manifest, using the stored model, bootstrap, diagnostic, table, and source-data files; and
read the H01 results report alongside its full-precision source tables rather than inferring numeric values from figure pixels.

Changes to shared metric preparation must be made upstream and propagated to every affected hypothesis. A display-only change can instead be made from the stored reporting objects without refitting the models or repeating the bootstrap.






TipReader takeaway



The H01 result comes from two verified model-data bundles, a single declared 17-response implementation, exact response-specific model frames, four complete multiplicity families, stored joint-refit bootstrap draws, and separate diagnostic and sensitivity records. This page connects those pieces without changing the scientific result.

title: Preparation 07: Inspect example days from each study site
text:
This final preparation page is a display-only inspection of the prepared one-minute data. It shows one participant-day from each study site before any hypothesis model is fitted. The profiles combine melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI; lx), local daylight, diary-defined periods, and declared non-wear so that readers can see what the accepted minute-level records look like.

Eligibility and selection rules
A participant-day could enter the selection pool only if it passed the general coverage rules from Preparation 02: at least 50% valid observations within each summarized hour and at least 80% valid observations across the full 24-hour day. title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
text:
The Visual Light Sensitivity Questionnaire (VLSQ-8) measures self-reported visual light sensitivity; higher scores indicate greater sensitivity according to the accepted scale.
The preregistered hypothesis was:

H8: Duration-, exposure-history-, and level-based metrics are associated with VLSQ-8 light sensitivity scores.

The analytical question is whether VLSQ-8 is associated with repeated participant-day personal light-exposure metrics after adjustment for study site. A participant-day is one participant’s eligible local calendar day. The primary near-eye sensor position more closely represents light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is not an ocular-exposure measure and is not pooled with near-eye measurements. Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) describes light in terms of melanopsin-weighted visual-system sensitivity.
Reported effects compare VLSQ-8 scores separated by one participant-level standard deviation (SD), equal to 5.540 points. Time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep is reported as an absolute difference in hours; the eight log-link outcomes are reported as ratios and corresponding percentage changes, on a separate scale. A back-transformed estimate returns a fitted coefficient to its stated hour-difference, ratio, or percentage-change scale. A 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes the uncertainty around that effect; Wald construction is named where relevant.
The site-average association is an average across sites that gives each site equal weight. The separate VLSQ-8-by-site interaction allows the association between VLSQ-8 and a light metric to differ by study site. False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment is applied within each declared nine-metric family.






NoteAnswer in brief



Across nine light-exposure metrics, neither the primary near-eye site-average associations nor their VLSQ-8-by-site interactions met the FDR-adjusted criterion. The strongest near-eye directional pattern was lower corrected melEDI dose per VLSQ-8 SD (ratio 0.846, 95% CI 0.716–0.999; raw p = 0.051, FDR-adjusted p = 0.160), so it is not an FDR-retained finding. Complementary chest results and the central sensitivity analyses did not change that conclusion, although site influence and specified model limitations require caution.

title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
text:
The preregistered hypothesis was:

H8: Duration-, exposure-history-, and level-based metrics are associated with VLSQ-8 light sensitivity scores.

The analytical question is whether participant-level self-reported visual light sensitivity is associated with repeated participant-day personal light-exposure metrics after adjustment for study site. Near-eye measurements are primary because they more closely represent light near the eyes during wear. Chest measurements provide complementary evidence and are not pooled with the near-eye measurements.






NoteResults in brief



Across nine light-exposure metrics, neither the primary near-eye average associations nor their site-specific heterogeneity met the multiplicity-adjusted criterion. The strongest near-eye directional pattern was lower corrected melEDI dose per VLSQ-8 SD (ratio 0.846, 95% CI 0.716–0.999; raw p = 0.051, BH-adjusted p = 0.160), so it is not a multiplicity-retained finding. Complementary chest results and the central sensitivity analyses did not change that conclusion, although site influence and specified model limitations require caution.








NoteExact-zero normalization audit



Shared decision METRIC-011 normalised eight primary L10 participant-day round-off remnants to exact zero (three near eye and five chest). A bounded H08 reseal updated only inherited L10 branches and the four affected BH families. It changed no displayed effect, p-value, retained decision, diagnostic disposition, sensitivity classification, or interpretation; all untargeted results and model objects passed the recorded reconciliation.

title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
text:
What was analysed
VLSQ-8 was available for all 184 participants across nine sites. The stored score equalled the sum of eight ordered 1–5 item codes plus 5 for every participant. Scores ranged from 13 to 39, with a mean of 21.598 and a participant SD of 5.540. The raw score was centred at the observed mean; no within-site standardisation was used.
Nine participant-day outcomes covered light level, duration, continuous periods, and exposure history. All use manuscript metric names and melEDI units. The longest continuous period is an observed lower bound unless its start and end are both exactly identified; that stricter definition is examined as a sensitivity.
The predefined preparation sensitivity is called the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. The name means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment; it does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored. For this one-time first explanation, the primary could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset because its approved preparation uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant. From here onward, it is called simply the primary dataset.

title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
text:
Statistical models
Participant-day models include a participant random intercept nested within site. This participant random effect represents remaining between-participant variation after site and VLSQ-8 are considered. Fixed site effects use the submitted site order and explicit sum contrasts, so the additive VLSQ-8 coefficient is the site-average slope rather than the slope at one reference site. The site-average likelihood-ratio test compares the site-only and additive models. A separate test compares the additive and interaction models to ask whether the VLSQ-8 association differs by site.
The following evaluated cell constructs every exact Wilkinson formula used for the principal comparisons and the two structured sensitivities, then presents their exact evaluated strings in one semantic table.

site_only <- stats::as.formula(
  "response_value ~ site + (1 | site:Id)"
)
additive <- stats::as.formula(
  "response_value ~ site + VLSQ8_c + (1 | site:Id)"
)
interaction <- stats::as.formula(
  "response_value ~ site * VLSQ8_c + (1 | site:Id)"
)
photoperiod_site_only <- stats::as.formula(
  "response_value ~ site + photoperiod_c + (1 | site:Id)"
)
photoperiod_additive <- stats::as.formula(
  "response_value ~ site + photoperiod_c + VLSQ8_c + (1 | site:Id)"
)
photoperiod_interaction <- stats::as.formula(
  "response_value ~ site * VLSQ8_c + photoperiod_c + (1 | site:Id)"
)
participant_site_only <- stats::as.formula(
  "participant_response ~ site"
)
participant_additive <- stats::as.formula(
  "participant_response ~ site + VLSQ8_c"
)
participant_interaction <- stats::as.formula(
  "participant_response ~ site * VLSQ8_c"
)

formula_names <- c(

)
accepted_formula_strings <- c(

  "response_value ~ site * VLSQ8_c + (1 | site:Id)",
  "response_value ~ site + photoperiod_c + (1 | site:Id)",
  "response_value ~ site + photoperiod_c + VLSQ8_c + (1 | site:Id)",
  "response_value ~ site * VLSQ8_c + photoperiod_c + (1 | site:Id)",
  "participant_response ~ site",
  "participant_response ~ site + VLSQ8_c",
  "participant_response ~ site * VLSQ8_c"

formula_objects_before_display <- mget(formula_names, inherits = FALSE)
formula_display <- tibble::tibble(
  Model = formula_names,
  `Evaluated Wilkinson formula` = unname(vapply(
    formula_objects_before_display,

title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
text:
Primary near-eye results
None of the nine average near-eye associations remained statistically supported after the complete FDR adjustment. Several point estimates suggested lower bright-light exposure at higher VLSQ-8 scores, but their uncertainty and family-adjusted evidence do not support a confirmatory claim.
The corrected melEDI-dose ratio was 0.846 per VLSQ-8 SD (95% CI 0.716–0.999). Its likelihood-ratio raw p was 0.051 and FDR-adjusted p was 0.160. title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
text:
Interpretation
On the accepted score, metric, sample, and model definitions, the observed data provide no FDR-adjusted evidence that VLSQ-8 score is associated with any of the nine primary near-eye personal light-exposure metrics. The complementary chest analyses and the central sensitivity analyses do not materially strengthen that evidence. Several estimates point toward lower bright-light exposure at higher scores, but their uncertainty, complete-family adjustment, and site influence make that directional pattern inconclusive.
This conclusion is not evidence that every true association is exactly zero, and the paired-placement comparison is not an equivalence test. The analysis is observational: it does not establish that visual light sensitivity changes personal light exposure, nor does it support physiological or health-effect claims.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns
text:
The preregistered hypothesis was:

“H11: Diurnal exposure patterns differ by sex.”

The recorded predictor is biological sex, coded Female or Male. Gender identity is a distinct construct and was not analysed. The analytical question is whether the fitted 24-hour personal melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) profile differs between participants recorded as Female and Male after accounting for site-specific temporal patterns, repeated observations within participants and days, and short-lag residual dependence.






TipAnswer in brief



After false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment, the primary near-eye Female-minus-Male curve differed globally (adjusted p = 0.028), and the complementary chest curve also differed globally (adjusted p = 0.029). The secondary level/shape analysis could not cleanly assign either globally supported curve to an independently resolved level or shape component; this does not overturn the global results. In the exploratory activity-complete sample, near eye was already unsupported before activity adjustment (raw p = 0.160) and remained unsupported after it (raw p = 0.364). At chest, the corresponding raw p-value changed from 0.025 to 0.050. This sensitivity is compatible with attenuation but cannot identify activity as a mechanism. Model checks classified all accepted fits as acceptable with specified limitations.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns
text:
What was analysed
The near-eye sensor position is primary because it measures the light field closer to the eyes. The chest sensor position is analysed separately as complementary evidence and is not a measure of ocular exposure. The placements are neither pooled nor treated as independent replicates. The response is the 30-minute arithmetic mean melEDI, modelled as log10(melEDI + 0.1).
The estimand is the complete fitted Female-minus-Male 24-hour curve at equal clock-time weighting. Its site-average fitted mean averages across included sites and gives each site equal weight. The participant is the independent unit for robust inference. A participant-day is one participant’s included observations on one local calendar day.

The primary near-eye model contains 141 participants (79 Female, 62 Male), 816 participant-days, 37,756 30-minute observations, and all nine sites. The chest model contains 154 participants (86 Female, 68 Male), 902 participant-days, 41,842 observations, and eight sites. These are the accepted temporal-model samples; no extra H11-specific row deletion was applied.






NoteKey terms





Site-average fitted mean: the fitted mean averaged across included sites, with each site given equal weight.

Complete-curve test: one joint test of the time-constant and time-varying Female-minus-Male contributions across the whole 24-hour curve.

Pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI): uncertainty for one displayed clock bin; it is not a simultaneous band across the full day.

Shifted-value ratio: both fitted melEDI values are shifted by the model’s 0.1-lx offset before the Female-to-Male ratio is calculated.

AR(1): a representation of autocorrelation in which residual similarity is stronger for measurements closer together in time.

Symlog: a display scale that is linear from 0 to 1 lx and base-10 logarithmic above 1 lx, with labels retained in original units.



Model and inference
The nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) allows the daily melEDI pattern to vary smoothly and nonlinearly over clock time. Its cyclic common daily curve and cyclic Female-specific deviation join smoothly across midnight. The model also includes site-specific temporal deviations, participant-specific time curves, and participant-day random effects. The latter two represent remaining repeated-measure variation after the shared time, biological-sex, and site structure is considered.
Autocorrelation is residual similarity between measurements close together in time. An AR(1) structure represents this dependence as stronger at shorter lags. Sequence starts prevent that correlation from crossing participant-day or gap boundaries. The detailed estimation and robust-covariance specification is documented in the preparation and provenance companion.
The following evaluated R cell reads and prints the exact Wilkinson formula supplied to every accepted H11 full model. Here, response is the transformed melEDI outcome and Male is the reference level.

accepted_h11_formula <- stats::as.formula(formula_registry$formula[[1L]])
accepted_h11_formula

response ~ sex + s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) + s(time_hour, 
    by = sex_smooth, bs = "cc", k = 12) + s(time_hour, site, 
    bs = "sz", k = 12) + s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", 
    k = 10) + s(participant_day, bs = "re")


The complete-curve, or global, test jointly evaluates the time-constant and time-varying contributions to the 48-bin Female-minus-Male curve. It produces one decision per placement and dataset. FDR adjustment is applied within separately labelled test families. Each global family has one test. The planned level and shape attribution tests form a separate two-test FDR family within each placement. Those secondary tests do not repeat the global test, and failure to resolve either component does not invalidate a supported global curve.
All curve and contrast intervals are participant-cluster-robust pointwise 95% CIs. Each applies to one displayed clock bin and does not support a simultaneous significant-period claim.

The registered hourly geometric-mean outcome, a fitted common-placement sample, an all-zero-inclusive preparation, and alternative temporal model forms remain unresolved. title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns
text:
Interpretation
These data support a biological-sex difference in the complete fitted daily melEDI profile at near-eye level, with complementary support at chest level. Near-eye pointwise estimates indicate the largest relative separation around the morning, whereas the chest contrast is nearly time-constant. However, the planned component analysis cannot attribute the supported joint result specifically to a level or shape component after multiplicity adjustment. That attribution limitation does not weaken the definition or validity of the separate global curve test.
Activity adjustment did not yield a supported adjusted global curve on the activity-complete sample at either placement. For near eye, however, the same-sample unadjusted curve was already unsupported, so the change cannot be assigned to activity. For chest, the curve magnitude changed modestly and the raw p-value moved just above 0.050. Neither pattern establishes mediation or a causal activity pathway.
The effect-size summaries are modest on the fitted model scale, and all clock- specific confidence intervals are pointwise. The result is therefore evidence for an overall structured association, not proof of a significant clock period, not an equivalence or placement-difference analysis, and not evidence that biological sex causally determines light exposure. Differences may reflect behavioural, occupational, environmental, or other correlated factors that this observational model does not identify.

title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
NoteAbout this analysis record



This page explains how verified Visual Light Sensitivity Questionnaire (VLSQ-8) scores and personal light-exposure metrics were turned into the H08 results. Higher VLSQ-8 scores indicate greater self-reported visual light sensitivity according to the accepted scale. The companion H08 results report presents the scientific findings.

title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
Purpose
H08 asks whether nine duration-, exposure-history-, and level-based personal light-exposure metrics are associated with VLSQ-8 visual-light-sensitivity scores. The primary near-eye sensor position more closely represents light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is not an ocular-exposure measure and is not pooled with near-eye measurement. Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) expresses light in terms of melanopsin-weighted visual-system sensitivity. Every inferential outcome has one row per participant-day, defined as one participant’s eligible local calendar day.
Reported effects compare VLSQ-8 scores separated by one participant-level standard deviation (SD), equal to 5.540 points. Time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep is reported as an absolute difference in hours; the other eight log-link outcomes use ratios and corresponding percentage changes. A back-transformed estimate returns a fitted coefficient to its stated hour difference, ratio, or percentage-change scale. A 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes uncertainty; Wald construction is named where relevant.
The site-average association averages across sites with equal weight. The separate VLSQ-8-by-site interaction allows the association between VLSQ-8 and a light metric to differ by site. False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment is applied within each declared complete nine-metric family.
The predefined preparation sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general requirement of at least 50% valid minutes per hour and at least 80% valid hours per day, but the timing of the remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For contrast at this first explanation, the primary could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset. Hereafter it is called simply the primary dataset.
This page identifies the exact data, score rule, samples, formulae, code, and stored checks behind the accepted report. It documents provenance; it does not create an alternate analysis.

text:
2. VLSQ-8 predictor
Scale and score reconstruction
VLSQ-8 contains eight ordered item codes from 1 to 5. For every participant, the stored score equalled the item sum plus 5. The constant offset does not affect a centred slope, but retaining it is necessary to reproduce the approved 13–39 score scale. All 184 participants had complete item and total scores. The score was centred at its observed participant mean, 21.598, and reported effects compare scores separated by the participant SD of 5.540 points. Scores were not standardised within site.

title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
3. Metrics and analytical samples
Metric definitions and missing values
The nine outcomes retain the manuscript names and melEDI units. Unsupported values remain missing; they are never converted to darkness or zero. Four metrics use Gaussian models after log10(value + 0.1) transformation, three non-negative duration metrics use Tweedie models with a log link, and two use Gaussian identity models. Practical effects are ratios except for time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep, which is an hour difference.
Current metric derivations are documented in Preparation 04, and the corresponding model-ready inputs in Preparation 06.
The longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI can be a lower bound when a remaining gap interrupts the observed period. A separate exact-identification sensitivity retains only participant-days for which both ends of the longest period are observed. The corrected melEDI dose uses the registered time-sensitive value; observed uncorrected dose is retained as a descriptive sensitivity on the same fitted sample.

title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
4. Model construction and inference
Exact formulae supplied to the models
The primary specification uses fixed site with sum-to-zero contrasts and a participant random intercept nested within site. This participant random effect represents remaining between-participant variation after site and VLSQ-8 are considered. The additive coefficient is therefore the site-average VLSQ-8 slope rather than a slope at one reference site. A likelihood-ratio comparison of the site-only and additive models tests the site-average association. Comparing the additive and interaction models tests the VLSQ-8-by-site interaction. Photoperiod adjustment and participant-level summary models are structured sensitivities. This separation is the current scientific choice recorded as DEV-035.
The table retains the exact evaluated Wilkinson formulae used for the current analysis and its two structured sensitivity branches.

Show the R code used for this displayanalysis_labels <- c(
  approved_participant_day = "Participant-day analysis",
  photoperiod_sensitivity = "Photoperiod sensitivity",
  participant_summary_sensitivity = "Participant-summary sensitivity"
)
role_labels <- c(
  site_only = "Site-only comparison",
  additive = "Additive VLSQ-8 model",
  interaction = "VLSQ-8-by-site interaction model"
)

formula_registry |>
  filter(.data$analysis_kind %in% names(analysis_labels)) |>
  mutate(
    Analysis = unname(analysis_labels[.data$analysis_kind]),
    `Model role` = unname(role_labels[.data$formula_id]),
    Formula = paste0("`", .data$formula, "`")
  ) |>
  select("Analysis", "Model role", "Formula") |>
  gt::gt(groupname_col = "Analysis") |>

  gt::cols_width(

Site-average association and VLSQ-8-by-site interaction tests were adjusted separately. Near-eye and chest placements and the primary and preparation-sensitivity datasets were also separate. text:
5. Diagnostics and influence
Every current additive and interaction fit was checked for convergence, Hessian status, singularity, fixed-effect rank, residual behaviour, response support, prediction bounds, and serial dependence. Exact response zeros and the expected zero mass were compared for Tweedie outcomes. The checks retain three explicit limitations: increasing residual spread for darkest 10 h mean, a small observed zero mass not reproduced for sleep time below 1 lx melEDI, and corrected-dose sensitivity to remaining-gap timing. No limitation was used as a significance screen.

6. Sensitivity analyses
Sensitivity branches preserve the accepted estimand unless their purpose explicitly changes sample construction, adjustment, or metric definition. They describe stability and do not promote an association that was not retained in the primary multiplicity family.
For the paired-placement and exact common-sample comparisons, the same participants and participant-days are used at both sensor positions, while near-eye and chest estimates are fitted separately. These are not equivalence tests or direct tests of a placement effect.

  summarise(
    fits = n(),
    converged = sum(.data$converged),
    full_rank = sum(.data$fixed_full_rank)
  )

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns
text:
Exploratory activity-context sensitivity
The accepted global test remains unadjusted for activity. An exploratory sensitivity asked whether the estimated Female-minus-Male curve changed after adding the recorded hourly activity context. To separate adjustment from sample selection, the accepted H11 model was first refitted without activity on the exact activity-complete sample and then refitted with activity on those same observations.
Diary hours were eligible only when exactly one activity was selected. Hours with multiple selections, no selection, all missing responses, or only an unspecified “other” activity were excluded rather than duplicated across categories. The retained contexts were home (reference), sleep, road or vehicle, indoor work, and outdoor activity. A 30-minute exposure observation was attached only when it lay wholly within one unique diary hour. This restriction produced the following exact samples.

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure
text:
The preregistered hypothesis was:

“H7: There is a ceiling (nonlinear) effect of absolute latitude and photoperiod on level-, duration-, and exposure-history-based light metrics.”

Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) is an illuminance-like measure weighted for melanopic photoreception and expressed in lux (lx). The primary near-eye sensor position places the wearable sensor near the eyes; the complementary chest sensor position is torso-worn and is not a measure of ocular exposure.
This report asks the part of that question that these data can address: is a pooled association between civil photoperiod and each planned personal light-exposure metric visible, and does the fitted association change from a locally supported increase to a slope that remains statistically compatible with zero through the longest recorded photoperiod?






NoteAnswer in brief



A qualifying transition from increase to a sustained near-flat tail was visible for six of nine primary near-eye metrics: mean melEDI, brightest 10 h mean, darkest 10 h mean, time above 1,000 lx melEDI, time above 250 lx melEDI during wake, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 14.24–16.20 h of civil photoperiod. The complementary chest analysis showed the pattern for seven of nine metrics: mean melEDI, darkest 10 h mean, both above-threshold durations, time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 13.01–18.47 h. These are visible pooled-data patterns under the qualifying-transition rule, not evidence that a physiological or environmental ceiling exists. No physiological or environmental ceiling was identified. Absolute latitude cannot be separated from site in this design, and site, collection period, incomplete photoperiod overlap, model form, and influential sites materially limit interpretation.

title: H07: Photoperiod and possible plateaus in personal light exposure
text:
The preregistered hypothesis was:

“H7: There is a ceiling (nonlinear) effect of absolute latitude and photoperiod on level-, duration-, and exposure-history-based light metrics.”

This report asks the part of that question that these data can address: is a pooled association between civil photoperiod and each planned personal light-exposure metric visible, and does the fitted association change from a pointwise detected increase to a derivative that remains statistically compatible with zero through the longest recorded photoperiod?






NoteAnswer in brief



A derivative-defined plateau pattern was visible for six of nine primary near-eye metrics: mean melEDI, brightest 10 h mean, darkest 10 h mean, time above 1,000 lx melEDI, time above 250 lx melEDI during wake, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 14.24–16.20 h of civil photoperiod. The complementary chest analysis showed the pattern for seven of nine metrics: mean melEDI, darkest 10 h mean, both above-threshold durations, time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 13.01–18.47 h. These are visible pooled-data patterns under a pointwise derivative rule, not evidence that a physiological or environmental ceiling exists. Absolute latitude cannot be separated from site in this design, and site, collection period, incomplete photoperiod overlap, model form, and influential sites materially limit interpretation.

title: H07: Photoperiod and possible plateaus in personal light exposure
text:
What was analysed
All nine planned metrics were analysed independently of fitted results from other hypotheses. Near-eye measurements are primary because they more closely represent light near the eyes; chest measurements provide complementary evidence. The placements were modelled separately. A common-sample sensitivity uses the same participants and participant-days for both placements, but it does not test or establish placement equivalence.
The primary dataset retains the approved metric-specific treatment of gaps. A predefined sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. The term means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment; it does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored. For this contrast only, the approved primary preparation could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset, because it uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant to the metric. Below, it is called simply the primary dataset.
The analysis unit was a participant-day, with one observation for each available metric, participant, day, and placement. Repeated days were handled with a participant random-effect smooth nested within site. The main near-eye samples span 15 August 2023 to 19 October 2025; chest samples span 14 May 2024 to 19 October 2025. Exact metric-specific counts are reported with each placement below.

title: H07: Photoperiod and possible plateaus in personal light exposure
text:
Model and plateau rule
Each metric and placement used a separate generalized additive model fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. The reported model was:
Show R codeformula_registry |>
  filter(.data$model_id == "adapted_photoperiod_smooth") |>
  pull(.data$formula) |>
  cat()
response_value ~ s(photoperiod_hours, k = 6, bs = “tp”) + s(site, bs = “re”) + s(site_participant, bs = “re”)
Here, response_value is the response shown in the specification table, photoperiod_hours is civil photoperiod, site is the study site, and site_participant identifies a participant within site. The smooth used a thin-plate regression spline with basis dimension k = 6. A broader k = 10 smooth and a model treating site as a fixed effect were fitted as model-form sensitivities.
Absolute latitude is fixed within site. It is therefore structurally confounded with site, and a latitude-by-photoperiod surface cannot separately identify a latitude association while accounting for site. The planned joint surface was inspected as an identifiability check but is not used for inference or for the plateau classification. No temperature or other unplanned environmental predictor was added.
For each reported smooth, the first derivative was evaluated at 100 equally spaced values over that metric’s exact recorded photoperiod range. Central finite differences used a step of 0.01 h, with one-sided differences at the two boundaries. Unconditional model-coefficient covariance produced pointwise 95% confidence intervals on the model’s linear-predictor scale.
A derivative-defined plateau pattern required all three conditions:

the lower pointwise 95% confidence limit for the derivative was above zero at one or more photoperiod values;
a later grid point had a 95% confidence interval containing zero; and
every subsequent interval through the longest recorded photoperiod also contained zero.

The reported transition is the bracket from the last pointwise detected increase to the first point of the sustained zero-compatible tail. This is the requested change from a statistically supported positive derivative to a non-significant derivative that remains non-significant to the end of the recorded range. The rule does not define a scientifically negligible slope, prove equivalence to zero, locate a true asymptote, or demonstrate a mechanism. The 100 pointwise checks and the nine cross-metric classifications were not multiplicity-adjusted; the classification is therefore descriptive.

Model checks
All 18 reported models converged. Gradients were small and all reported Hessian minima were positive. This does not prove temporal independence, but it did not indicate a strong residual day-to-day process after participant clustering.

The expanded-basis sensitivity therefore carries more weight than a single diagnostic threshold: it reproduced 16 of 17 evaluable classifications, with one near-eye fit failing its Hessian check and the chest sleep low-light classification changing.

title: H07: Photoperiod and possible plateaus in personal light exposure
text:
Interpretation
The pooled analysis shows several fitted photoperiod associations that rise and then meet the prespecified pointwise rule for a sustained zero-compatible derivative. The recurring patterns for mean melEDI, darkest 10 h mean, both above-threshold duration metrics, and melEDI dose across the two placements are the most consistent descriptive findings. Brightest 10 h mean differs by placement, the longest-period result is sensitive to sample definition and model form, and the chest sleep low-light result is undermined by distributional failure, common-row analyses, model-form changes, and site influence.
The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore that derivative-defined plateau patterns are visible for several personal light-exposure metrics in the pooled data, subject to substantial design and model limitations. The results do not establish a ceiling, an equivalence region, a causal effect of photoperiod, a distinct latitude effect, a health or clinical consequence, or equivalence between near-eye and chest placement.
Exact input identities, metric-specific model frames, evaluated formulas, diagnostic provenance, code order, and output identities are documented in the H07 analysis preparation and provenance companion.
Models were fitted with R 4.6.1, mgcv 1.9.4, and gratia 0.11.2.

title: H03: Self-reported light source and measured personal light exposure
text:
The preregistered hypothesis was:

H3: Hourly self-reported light exposure categories predict hourly geometric mean melanopic EDI.

For each accepted participant-hour, participants reported one primary light source. This analysis asks whether the seven registered categories are associated with measured one-hour melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) after accounting for study site.






NoteAnswer in brief



The seven light-source categories were associated with near-eye melEDI, F(6, 139) = 97.54, p <0.001. The association between light-source category and melEDI was allowed to differ by study site in a category-by-site interaction model. Because that interaction was supported, descriptive category and site summaries come from this model; only the preregistered primary omnibus comes from the additive population-mean model. Outdoor daylight had the highest site-average near-eye melEDI, while sleep darkness had the lowest. Supported site-specific deviations showed that the magnitude of the category association varied materially across study sites.
Complementary chest summaries had the same broad ordering for the six categories for which a site-average estimate could be calculated across all eight chest sites. A site-average estimate for external light during sleep could not be calculated because one chest site-category cell was absent. The gap-timing-unaware dataset did not change the primary omnibus conclusion or any primary category classification.
