text:
Site dependence
The work/free association differed across study sites (FDR-adjusted p = 0.017). Activity and previous sleep had no FDR-retained predictor-by-site interaction. In the interaction model, the site-average work/free ratio, calculated with equal weight for each site, was 1.15 (95% CI 0.93–1.44), compared with 1.45 in the common-effect model. The interaction model’s site-average day-type association did not meet the adjusted threshold (three-predictor FDR-adjusted p = 0.298). Day type also did not meet the adjusted threshold when the working variance changed (FDR-adjusted p = 0.260). The day-type conclusion is therefore site- and model-dependent.

The work/free association differed across sites (FDR-adjusted p = 0.017). Activity and previous sleep had no FDR-retained site interaction. The primary 1.45 work/free ratio comes from a model that constrains this association to be common across sites; it is not the average of the ratios from the interaction model. In the interaction model, the site-average ratio is the geometric mean of the nine site ratios: 1.15 (95% CI 0.93–1.44). Three sites are above that average and six are below it because three larger positive log-scale departures balance six smaller negative departures. This is not an algebraic inconsistency, but the attenuation from 1.45 to 1.15 shows that the work/free conclusion depends on model structure. The interaction-model site averages remain close to the common-effect results for activity (1.93 versus 2.06) and previous sleep (0.97 versus 0.98).

text:
Sensitivity and complementary sensor evidence
The required gap-timing-unaware dataset uses the same 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules as the primary dataset, but does not use the timing of the remaining within-hour and within-day gaps for a metric-specific adjustment. The primary analysis could therefore be interpreted as time-sensitive. The near-eye estimates were stable under this dataset change, including on exact common hours. Complementary chest estimates had similar directions.
The paired-day comparison used the same 109 participants and 553 participant-days at both sensor positions, but three hourly keys differed at each position. It is not an observation-level identity comparison, an equivalence analysis, or a direct sensor-position effect. Activity and previous-sleep conclusions were stable across the declared checks. Day type remained sensitive to the working variance and to omission of some sites.
A separate near-eye-only sensitivity excluded participants recorded as not employed or marginally employed. It retained all nine sites and classified all three primary associations as stable within model uncertainty.

Show complementary placement and sensitivity results
Required dataset sensitivity
The gap-timing-unaware sensitivity applies the comparison defined above to the same three predictors and sensor positions.
The all-available near-eye comparison contains 16,329 hours from 702 participant-days, 137 participants, and nine sites. On the exact common-hour frame, 16,329 hour keys remain and only 12 response values differ. The three near-eye ratios are stable: 1.44 for free/work, 2.08 for active/sedentary, and 0.96 per additional hour of sleep. The work/free site interaction also remains FDR-retained (FDR-adjusted p = 0.015).

text:
Exploratory diary and clock-time analyses
Exercise location, active travel, sedentary time, sleep onset, and final wake time are descriptive extensions fitted one at a time. They do not select or rescue the primary model. The nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the association with local clock time to bend across the day and is separate from the primary average associations. Its pointwise 95% CI applies to one displayed time. It is not a simultaneous band or a multiplicity-controlled whole-curve test.
Active status was higher from about 07:15 to 19:00 and lower from about 23:30 to 05:15 across midnight, when estimated melEDI was low. The free-day curve was lower from about 06:45 to 09:15 and from 18:45 to 19:15. These windows exclude the null ratio 1 on the local 15-minute grid, but they do not define confirmatory significant time segments.

Nonlinear time-of-day GAM analysis
The exploratory nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the associations with local clock time to bend across the day. It separates occurrence (melEDI greater than zero, binomial-logit) from positive magnitude (Gamma-log); multiplying their response-scale means gives estimated hourly melEDI. Both components use four cyclic factor-by clock smooths for work/free day × activity status, with one smoothing parameter shared across the four curves. Study site enters as a fixed adjustment only; there is no site-specific clock smooth and no sz component. Participant and participant-day random-effect smooths, true-sequence AR.start, and residual working correlations remain. The chosen basis is k = 16, fitted with bam(method = "fREML", discrete = TRUE).

title: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure
text:
Interpretation and limitations
The common-effect results describe observational associations with estimated mean hourly near-eye melEDI among observed hours that met the support criteria. They do not establish causal effects and do not answer the broader preregistered question about daily light-exposure metrics. Participant-days with more retained participant-hours contribute more weight.
The free/work result is qualified by its predictor-by-site interaction, the smaller site-average estimate from that interaction model, the alternative working-variance result, and leave-one-site-out checks. Chest and paired-day analyses provide complementary non-ocular context, not sensor-position equivalence or a direct placement effect. Participant-cluster-robust inference allows within-participant dependence, but it does not remove residual time-of-day structure or repair an imperfect mean model. The nonlinear GAM analysis is exploratory; its pointwise intervals apply to individual displayed hours and do not support simultaneous whole-curve claims.

Detailed analysis record
This section retains the exact fitted samples, model formulas, declared FDR families, linked source data, and technical provenance for auditing.
Outcome, predictors, sensor positions, and fitted samples
The primary outcome is the zero-aware geometric mean melEDI for each retained participant-hour at the near-eye sensor position. A participant-hour is one observed one-hour interval from one participant that met the support criteria defined in Preparation 06. Activity is binary: sedentary means no reported exercise, while active includes light, moderate, or vigorous reported exercise. Day type and activity are participant-day diary variables, where a participant-day is one calendar day contributed by one participant; previous sleep duration is linked from the preceding sleep period. Because participant-days contribute 19–24 supported participant-hours, the estimand is participant-hour weighted rather than participant-day weighted.

The primary fit contains 16,596 supported hours from 715 participant-days, 137 participants, and nine study sites. The smallest primary site × category cells contain 185 hours, 8 participant-days, and 4 participants; these minima do not all occur in the same cell. Download the exact category cell registry.
The TUM exercise-diary identity check uses the pinned immutable melidosData 1.0.6 object and finds 7 S001 rows and 0 S101 rows, with no local identifier rewrite. The KNUST_S005 numeral 3,600 is interpreted as 3,600 seconds, or one sedentary hour, only for eligible exploratory analyses; it is not added to the primary analysis.
For the required sensitivity analysis, the gap-timing-unaware dataset applies the same 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules but does not use the timing of remaining missing observations for a metric-specific adjustment. The primary analysis could therefore be interpreted as time-sensitive. Both datasets are defined in Preparation 06. Hereafter, the corrected input is called the primary dataset.
Models and inference
The common-effect model is a zero-inclusive quasi-Poisson generalized linear model with a log link and fixed study-site terms. A participant-cluster-robust 95% confidence interval (95% CI) allows observations from the same participant to be related and uses the HC3 small-sample correction. Participants, rather than participant-hours, are therefore the inferential replicates. One-coefficient tests use a t reference with 136 degrees of freedom.
The predictor-by-site interaction model allows the association of day type, activity, or previous sleep with hourly melEDI to differ by study site. Its site-interaction blocks use Wald F tests with restriction-rank and 136 denominator degrees of freedom. A site-average estimate averages across the nine sites with equal weight for each site on the linear-predictor scale before back-transformation.

Exploratory analyses
Nonlinear local-clock GAM analysis
Time of day is described separately from the three primary average associations. This nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the associations with local clock time to bend across the day. It has two parts: a binomial model for whether hourly melEDI is positive and a Gamma log-link model for the positive magnitude. Their response-scale product gives estimated mean hourly melEDI.

The occurrence basis check remains a warning: its k-check p-values are small, although effective degrees of freedom remain below the basis ceiling. The lower-basis comparison changes some response-scale curves. Together with occurrence calibration, residual working correlation, and omitted cross-component covariance, this prevents confirmatory whole-curve inference. title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure
text:
The signed hypothesis states: “Day type (weekday/weekend; free/work day), daily exercise, and sleep variables predict daily light exposure metrics.” This complementary analysis asks that question with one row per admissible metric-specific participant-day. It does not give days with more supported hours greater weight.
The completed hourly H06 analysis is the selected main H06 result. This participant-day analysis is complementary, preregistration-oriented evidence. The two analyses are related but have different outcomes and weighting; neither result substitutes for the other. The analysis-preparation and provenance companion documents the exact inputs, models, checks, and stored outputs used here.






NoteAnswer in brief



In the primary near-eye analysis, false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment, which limits the expected proportion of false discoveries within each prespecified 15-slot family, retained associations for 10 of 14 estimable metrics with Free versus Work day, 6 of 14 with Active versus Sedentary status, and 12 of 14 per additional hour of previous-night sleep. Every retained association requires the model-check qualifications (model diagnostics), which assess fit, support, residual behavior, and sensitivity evidence, described below.
For outcomes fitted as \log_{10}(Y + 0.1), Y remains in its stated unit, such as lx for melEDI, h for continuous periods, or lx h for dose. The back-transformed ratios compare fitted geometric-mean-like values of Y + 0.1; they are not ratios of raw metric means.

Free days had lower fitted mean melEDI, M10 mean, waking time above 250 lx melEDI, longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose than Work days. M10 and L10 midpoints and first light above 250 lx melEDI were later, whereas last light above 250 lx melEDI was earlier.
Active days had higher fitted mean melEDI, M10 mean, time above 1,000 and 250 lx melEDI, longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose than Sedentary days.
Longer previous-night sleep was associated with lower fitted light-level, bright-duration, longest-period, and dose metrics; more time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep; and later M10, L10, mean-light, and first-light timing.

Ten primary predictor-by-site interaction blocks, which allow an association to differ among sites, met their separate 15-slot FDR rule. For example, the interaction model estimated lower Free-day mean melEDI at every site, with pointwise 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) excluding 1 at Dortmund (DE), Tübingen (DE), Madrid (ES), and Kumasi (GH). A pointwise interval assesses one site estimate at a time and is not a simultaneous band. The global interaction test establishes variation across sites, while the site intervals describe where the fitted site-specific contrasts are clearest.
In the exploratory mutually adjusted daily models, activity estimates were stable after adding day type and sleep. Three sleep estimates and four work/free estimates shifted by 1 to less than 2 standard errors. One work/free estimate, time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, reversed direction and shifted by more than 3 standard errors. Mean melEDI nevertheless remained lower on Free days after adjustment, with a fitted ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.82; FDR q < 0.001).
The separate nonlinear generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) analysis of 30-minute bins allowed context associations to vary smoothly over clock time while accounting for repeated measurements. It found time-varying profiles for day type, activity, within-participant sleep, and between-participant sleep in its four-test exploratory FDR family. The selected main hourly H06 analysis does not give the same answer as the daily mean metric: hourly melEDI was higher on Free days, whereas the participant-day mean metric was lower. This difference is scientifically plausible because the analyses use different outcomes, weighting, and model structures.
The overall two-part L10 mean result remains non-estimable, and all three primary MDER 95% intervals included zero. The gap-timing-unaware analysis is reported only as a sensitivity.

title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure
text:
Data and analysis
Outcomes, contexts, and sample roles
The 15 participant-day outcomes comprise mean melEDI; M10 and L10 mean melEDI; four threshold-duration measures; the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI; M10 and L10 midpoint; mean, first, and last timing above 250 lx melEDI; melEDI dose; and melanopic daylight efficacy ratio (MDER). “Period” describes the continuous-duration metric. Sleep-period light is interpreted as the bedside sleep environment, not verified ocular exposure.
The three primary contexts were:

Free versus Work day;
Active versus Sedentary daily activity status; and
each additional hour of previous-night sleep duration, centered at 8 h.

Near-eye measurements are primary. All-available chest results are a complementary non-ocular comparison. Paired/common results compare the two placements after retaining the same participant-days in both placements. More generally, a common sample means that the compared models or placements use the same participant-days. The gap-timing-unaware dataset repeats the near-eye analysis as a separate metric-construction sensitivity.

Ranges arise because every metric × predictor result uses its exact complete fitted frame. Exact denominators accompany every result below.








The nine study sites, in display order, are Borås (SE), Delft (NL), Dortmund (DE), Tübingen (DE), Munich (DE), Madrid (ES), Izmir (TR), San José (CR), Kumasi (GH). Primary near-eye results use all nine sites; the complementary chest and paired/common results use eight sites where both the placement and exact metric-specific frame are supported.
Models, contrasts, and multiplicity
The non-timing outcomes use fixed study-site terms and a participant random intercept, which allows participants to have different baseline outcome levels. The primary models were fitted separately for each predictor, so their estimates are not mutually adjusted for the other two day-level contexts. The common-association and predictor-by-site interaction formulas are:
response ~ site + predictor + (1 | participant)
response ~ site * predictor + (1 | participant)
Four clock outcomes, M10 midpoint, L10 midpoint, first timing above 250 lx melEDI, and last timing above 250 lx melEDI, use the corresponding fixed-site linear models with participant-cluster HC3 uncertainty. All displayed intervals are pointwise 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs); each assesses one estimate at a time, and none is simultaneous. A site-average estimate gives each included site equal weight, irrespective of its observed sample size.
Multiplicity comprises 12 separate FDR families: primary and gap-timing-unaware datasets × three predictors × association or predictor-by-site interaction. Every family retains all 15 named metric slots. L10 mean remains the non-estimable slot 3 with missing raw and adjusted p-values; MDER occupies slot 15 and has no association FDR support.

NoteHow to read the estimates




A site-average estimate gives every included site equal weight. It is not weighted by the number of observations contributed by each site.
A predictor-by-site interaction allows the association between a context and an outcome to differ among sites. A global interaction test does not by itself identify which site estimates differ.
A pointwise 95% CI describes uncertainty for one displayed estimate. It is not a simultaneous interval across sites, metrics, or clock times.
An FDR adjustment limits the expected proportion of false discoveries among the tests in its explicitly defined family.
A participant random intercept allows participants to have different baseline outcome levels. A common sample retains the same participant-days across the compared models or placements.

Model checks cover fit, support, residual behavior, and sensitivity evidence. A working first-order autoregressive correlation, AR(1), allows adjacent residuals within a participant-day sequence to be correlated.

An adjustment factor below 1 means that the site’s fitted ratio is lower than the site-average ratio; a factor above 1 means it is higher. Multiplying the site-average ratio by the adjustment factor recovers the site’s full fitted ratio. For the author’s mean-melEDI example, the site-average Free/Work ratio from the interaction model was 0.70 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.78), with every site weighted equally. Complete site-specific interaction estimates
The L10 occurrence component had complete or quasi-complete separation, so the overall two-part association and predictor-by-site interaction tests were not estimable. Positive-only and regularized component model checks do not replace that overall result. MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable positive finite one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios; its primary estimates were −0.001 for Free versus Work day (95% CI −0.013 to 0.011), 0.008 for Active versus Sedentary (−0.007 to 0.024), and 0.002 per additional hour of sleep (−0.003 to 0.006).

Exploratory mutually adjusted daily analysis
This exploratory batch directly addresses whether day type, activity, and previous-night sleep remain stable when included together. For each metric, one common complete-case near-eye frame was used for both the separate predictor models and the mutually adjusted model. For the 14 estimable metrics, this common sample contains 715 participant-days from 137 participants. Using the same rows prevents a sample change from being mistaken for covariate adjustment.
For non-timing outcomes, the mutually adjusted formula was:
response ~ site + day type + activity + previous-night sleep +
  (1 | participant)
The predictor-by-site interaction models added one site × context block at a time while holding the other two contexts additive. This is the prespecified lower-dimensional implementation of the proposed site * day type + site * activity + site * sleep duration structure. It preserves all three main context terms but evaluates each interaction block without conditioning it on two other high-dimensional interaction blocks. The four timing outcomes used the corresponding fixed-site linear models with participant-cluster HC3 covariance. L10 mean remained the named non-estimable slot 3 and was not replaced. title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure
text:
Exploratory 30-minute time-of-day GAMM
This separate analysis asks how the shape of the 24-hour profile varies by day type, activity, and sleep. It is not a daily-metric sensitivity. The response is the 30-minute arithmetic mean melEDI, Y, transformed as \log_{10}(Y + 0.1\ \mathrm{lx}). Its 33,057 supported half-hour bins come from 715 participant-days, 137 participants, and all nine sites.
The accepted mgcv::bam() model used Gaussian identity errors, fREML, discrete = TRUE, one thread, and a frame-specific working AR(1) coefficient. This working correlation allows adjacent residuals within each audited participant-day sequence to be correlated. Its exact smooth structure was:
s(time, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
s(time, day type, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
s(time, activity, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
s(time, by = between-participant sleep, k = 12) +
s(time, by = within-participant sleep, k = 12) +
s(time, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
s(time, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +
s(participant-day, bs = "re")
Only the global time smooth used the cyclic cubic basis. The sz, fs, and sleep time margins retained mgcv’s default thin-plate basis, with no cyclic xt request. Sleep was separated into the participant mean and the day’s deviation from that mean.

section: Comparison with the selected main H06 analysis
text:
Comparison with the selected main H06 analysis
The selected main H06 analysis and this complementary analysis do not estimate the same quantity. Main H06 gives each supported participant-hour one row and models the zero-aware geometric mean melEDI for that hour, with all three contexts in one model. H06_daily gives each admissible participant-day one row per metric. Its primary models are predictor-specific, while the exploratory joint column below uses a common 715-day frame and includes all three contexts. Where a global predictor-by-site interaction met its FDR rule, the table uses the site-average full contrast from that interaction model, with every site weighted equally, and gives the range of its nine full site-specific ratios. Otherwise it uses the additive model’s common contrast. The additive-family association q-value remains the prespecified association test, while the global interaction q-value determines which effect model is displayed.

Supported interaction rows use the site-average geometric mean of the nine full site-specific ratios from that model and show the site range. Other rows use the additive common contrast. Interaction-model site ratios are full contrasts and require no multiplication by a main effect. Numerical equality is neither expected nor claimed.








The clearest contrast is day type, for which all three global site interactions were supported. The interaction-model site-average ratio was 1.15 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.44) in main hourly H06, with full site-specific ratios from 0.53 to 2.44. Daily mean melEDI was lower on Free days in both the predictor-specific interaction model, site-average ratio 0.70 (0.63 to 0.78; site range 0.40 to 0.95), and the mutually adjusted interaction model, 0.73 (0.66 to 0.81; site range 0.44 to 1.00). This is not a failed replication. The hourly analysis weights days by their supported hours and targets a retained hour’s geometric mean; the daily analysis weights admissible days equally and targets a daily metric.
Activity was positive in all three analyses. Its primary daily interaction was supported, so that column uses the interaction-model site-average ratio 1.22 (1.08 to 1.39; full site ratios 0.84 to 2.26). The main hourly and mutually adjusted daily activity interactions were not supported, so their displayed 2.06 and 1.16 ratios come from additive models. Previous sleep had no supported site interaction in any column. It was compatible with little hourly association, additive ratio 0.98 and FDR q = 0.745, but was associated with lower daily mean melEDI, additive ratios 0.89 and 0.90. The analyses therefore provide related but non-interchangeable evidence about hourly exposure and participant-day metrics.

title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure
text:
Model checks and limitations
Primary and gap-sensitivity daily grid
All 468 non-L10 model cells passed the hard construct, support, numerical, and estimability gates, but every cell was classified acceptable with limitations after direct visual review of residual centering, variance, and gross distributional shape. No gross residual failure was observed.
Temporal dependence was retained as a mandatory model-check sidecar rather than an automatic failure criterion. Actual-date AR counterparts were sometimes singular, numerically unresolved, or left residual dependence; those findings remain part of interpretation but do not replace the primary estimates or p-values. In the primary timing route, the first-light Work/Free Student-t estimate shifted by 1.23 participant-cluster HC3 standard errors, and the L10 midpoint activity AR estimate shifted by 1.26 HC3 standard errors. Timing predictor-by-site results remain sensitivity-dependent.
Participant/site deletion checks were stable for 270 of 468 cells, showed a substantial limitation for 128, were unstable for 46, and had a non-estimable deletion refit for 24. Gaussian, Tweedie, Student-t, exact-period, and AR model-check sidecars are reported as response-family or stability limitations; none was used to substitute a p-value. MDER additionally retains its heavy-tail and site-influence qualifications.

Residual review and hard construct/support/numerical checks determine overall usability. AR, influence, family, and exact-period rows are mandatory nonblocking limitation sidecars under the analysis rule.








Exploratory mutually adjusted daily models
All 14 estimable joint models and their required additive and one-interaction structures were numerically estimable. Direct residual-plot review classified all 14 as review limitations and none as a gross failure. First-light timing retained a U-shaped residual pattern and heavy tails under the participant-HC3 route. MDER retained pronounced upper-tail and site-influence limitations. Actual-date residual lag was reported descriptively and did not replace or invalidate an otherwise usable model. No deletion batch, bootstrap, or simulation was added to this exploratory analysis.
Exploratory temporal GAMM
Five of six fitted frames met the accepted formula, convergence, basis, residual, temporal-dependence, fixed-term-identifiability, and cyclic-closure rules. All six BAM fits converged without fitting warnings, but the paired chest frame did not meet the residual-scale extraction rule and contributed no association summary. In the primary near-eye fit, the residual Q-Q correlation was 0.965, the absolute-residual/fitted Spearman correlation was 0.293, final pooled lag-1 correlation was 0.090, and the largest absolute site lag-1 correlation was 0.159. The bounded k = 16 check supported retaining k = 12. Participant and site deletion robustness remains untested for the GAMM, so its results stay exploratory.
These are observational associations with recorded day-level contexts. They do not establish causal effects, health outcomes, identical associations across sites, or equivalence between sensor placements.

title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure
H06 daily-metric analysis preparation and provenance
text:
This page explains how the complementary H06 participant-day analysis was prepared, fitted, checked, and translated into the reported tables and figures. The selected hourly H06 analysis remains the main H06 result. A participant-day is one eligible local calendar day from one participant. Each admissible light-exposure metric contributes at most one row for that participant-day, so days are not weighted by their number of supported hours.
The complementary H06 daily-metric results report contains the association estimates, confidence intervals, multiplicity decisions, site-specific patterns, complementary analyses, and the comparison with the selected main hourly H06 analysis.
crumbs: H06 complementary daily preparation and provenance

title: H06 daily-metric analysis preparation and provenance
text:
Analysis path
The primary path estimates each context separately for each daily metric. The predictor-by-site interaction path allows that association to differ among sites. Two exploratory paths then examine covariate stability and 30-minute clock-time profiles without changing the primary participant-day estimand. The nonlinear generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) analysis represents smooth clock-time variation while accounting for repeated measurements. Its working first-order autoregressive correlation, AR(1), allows adjacent residuals within a participant-day sequence to be correlated. A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) assesses one displayed estimate and is not a simultaneous band. Model checks assess fit, observed support, residual behavior, and sensitivity evidence.

For shifted-log outcomes, the fitted response is Z = \log_{10}(Y + 0.1), where Y remains in the metric’s stated unit, such as lx for melEDI, h for continuous periods, or lx h for dose. The back-transformed quantity is geometric-mean-like for Y + 0.1 in that unit; it is not the raw arithmetic mean of Y. The main response treatments were:


\log_{10}(Y + 0.1) for zero-containing right-skewed level, continuous- period, and dose outcomes selected for the shifted-log Gaussian route;
a Tweedie distribution with log link for non-negative duration outcomes with a point mass at zero and a continuous positive part;
identity-scale Gaussian models for outcomes whose residual behavior was judged adequate on that scale; and
clock hours for timing outcomes. L10 midpoint was unwrapped at 16:00 so that values after 16:00 and before the following morning occupy one continuous night-centred axis.

Exact zero handling was metric-specific. Exact zeros remained in every one-part model whose response allowed zero. For the darkest 10 h mean, exact zeros remained in the occurrence component and were excluded only from the strictly positive magnitude component. Its joint two-part association was not estimable because the occurrence component separated, so its named multiplicity slot remains missing. Daily melanopic daylight efficacy ratio (MDER) is the arithmetic mean of viable positive finite one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios. It requires at least 720 viable ratios on a complete 1,440-minute local wall-clock grid and is not a ratio of daily integrals.

response_value ~ site * predictor + (1 | participant_key)
Component-specific intervals only; joint association and heterogeneity tests are non-estimable


Fixed-site linear model with participant-cluster HC3 covariance
response_value ~ site
response_value ~ site + predictor
response_value ~ site * predictor
Participant-cluster HC3 covariance; participant clusters minus one degrees of freedom; pointwise 95% CI









The four timing outcomes repaired to participant-cluster HC3 inference are M10 midpoint, L10 midpoint, first timing above 250 lx melEDI, and last timing above 250 lx melEDI. Their fixed-site linear models use participant-cluster HC3 covariance with finite-cluster adjustment and participant-clusters-minus-one degrees of freedom. Other estimable daily outcomes use their selected Gaussian or Tweedie mixed model with a participant random intercept, which allows participants to have different baseline outcome levels.
The exact registered benchmark was retained without silent substitution:
response_value ~ predictor + (predictor | site) +
  (1 | site:participant_key)
It is a benchmark because nine sites provide limited support for a random site intercept, random predictor slope, and their correlation. The fixed-site route is the reported estimand. For categorical predictors it is the Free/Work or Active/Sedentary site-average contrast, with every site weighted equally. For previous sleep it is the association per additional hour, also averaged equally over sites. The interaction route reports the complete site-specific association, not an interaction adjustment that must be interpreted alone.

text:
Model checks, influence, and sensitivities
Three-class model-check architecture
Hard failure was reserved for an unavailable or non-estimable base result, convergence or Hessian failure, singularity, rank or covariance failure, invalid timing support, observed-response support failure, or visually confirmed gross residual behavior. Residual distribution was judged visually from residual-versus-fitted and Q–Q displays for Gaussian or HC3 fits. Tweedie fits used Pearson residual-versus-fitted displays and zero-mass and prediction- support checks; normal Pearson residuals were not required.
All 468 non-L10 metric-by-predictor-by-scenario cells had complete visual review and no gross visual or hard construct failure after the gap clock-unit repair. Each was retained as acceptable with limitations. Autocorrelation, participant or site deletion, exact-period, and response-family checks are mandatory row-linked sidecars. They qualify interpretation but do not by themselves fail an otherwise estimable result.

Exploratory jointly adjusted daily models
The exploratory covariate-stability analysis places work/free day, activity, and previous-night sleep in one model. Fourteen estimable metrics share the same primary near-eye common frame of 715 participant-days from 137 participants and nine sites; the non-estimable darkest 10 h joint outcome is retained as the named missing slot.

title: H06 daily-metric analysis preparation and provenance
text:
Exploratory 30-minute clock-time GAMM
The clock-time analysis has a different row and estimand. Its outcome Y is the arithmetic mean melEDI in an admissible 30-minute bin. The model response is Z = \log_{10}(Y + 0.1\ \mathrm{lx}). Exact zeros remain in this one-part Gaussian model. The displayed inverse transform, 10^\eta - 0.1, is a back-transform of the conditional mean log response. It is geometric-mean-like for Y+0.1 and is not raw-scale arithmetic E[Y].

    Response = paste(.data$response_source, .data$response_transform, sep = "; "),

    Estimand = .data$estimand,
    `Inverse-transform qualification` = .data$inverse_transform_qualification
  ) |>

Response
Family
Formula
Estimand

arithmetic_mean_medi_lx; log10(melEDI + 0.1 lx)
Gaussian; identity
response ~ s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) + s(time_hour, work_free_day,      bs = "sz", k = 12) + s(time_hour, activity_status, bs = "sz",      k = 12) + s(time_hour, by = sleep_between_h, k = 12) + s(time_hour,      by = sleep_within_h, k = 12) + s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz",      k = 12) + s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +      s(participant_day, bs = "re")
E[log10(30-minute arithmetic-mean melEDI + 0.1 lx) | local time, work/free day, daily activity status, within- and between-person previous-night sleep duration, site, participant, participant-day]
back-transform of a mean log response; geometric-mean-like and conditional-median scale, not raw-scale E[Y]








The model was fitted with mgcv::bam(), fREML, discrete = TRUE, one R thread, and global 0/24 knots. The global clock smooth is cyclic cubic with k=12. Work/free day, activity, and site use sum-to-zero factor smooths with k=12 and the default thin-plate time marginal, not a cyclic marginal. Participant uses a factor smooth with k=10, and participant-day uses a random intercept smooth. Previous sleep is separated into between-participant and within-participant smooth functions.
Rows are ordered by site, participant, local date, true source time, and clock bin. A working AR(1) sequence restarts at each participant-day and at every missing, non-one-to-one, or physically discontinuous true-time boundary. Each frame’s rho was estimated anew from its own preliminary full-model response residuals and then fixed for the final fit.

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure
text:
The preregistered hypothesis was:

“H7: There is a ceiling (nonlinear) effect of absolute latitude and photoperiod on level-, duration-, and exposure-history-based light metrics.”

Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) is an illuminance-like measure weighted for melanopic photoreception and expressed in lux (lx). The primary near-eye sensor position places the wearable sensor near the eyes; the complementary chest sensor position is torso-worn and is not a measure of ocular exposure.
This report asks the part of that question that these data can address: is a pooled association between civil photoperiod and each planned personal light-exposure metric visible, and does the fitted association change from a locally supported increase to a slope that remains statistically compatible with zero through the longest recorded photoperiod?






NoteAnswer in brief



A qualifying transition from increase to a sustained near-flat tail was visible for six of nine primary near-eye metrics: mean melEDI, brightest 10 h mean, darkest 10 h mean, time above 1,000 lx melEDI, time above 250 lx melEDI during wake, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 14.24–16.20 h of civil photoperiod. The complementary chest analysis showed the pattern for seven of nine metrics: mean melEDI, darkest 10 h mean, both above-threshold durations, time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 13.01–18.47 h. These are visible pooled-data patterns under the qualifying-transition rule, not evidence that a physiological or environmental ceiling exists. No physiological or environmental ceiling was identified. Absolute latitude cannot be separated from site in this design, and site, collection period, incomplete photoperiod overlap, model form, and influential sites materially limit interpretation.

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure
section: Data, sensor positions, metrics, and support
text:
Data, sensor positions, metrics, and support
All nine planned metrics were analysed independently of fitted results from other hypotheses. Near-eye measurements are primary because they more closely represent light near the eyes; chest measurements provide complementary evidence. The placements were modelled separately. A common-sample sensitivity uses the same participants and participant-days for both placements, but it does not test or establish placement equivalence.
The primary dataset retains the approved metric-specific treatment of gaps. A predefined sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. The term means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment; it does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored. For this contrast only, the approved primary preparation could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset, because it uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant to the metric. Below, it is called simply the primary dataset.
A participant-day is one participant’s available metric value on one local calendar date at one sensor position. Repeated days were handled with a participant random-effect smooth nested within site. Depending on the metric, the primary near-eye analysis contains 139–141 participants and 655–816 participant-days, whereas the complementary chest analysis contains 153–154 participants and 743–902 participant-days. The recorded civil-photoperiod support used by the metric-specific fits spans 10.33–20.52 h overall. title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure
text:
Reading guide

A nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the association between civil photoperiod and a light metric to bend rather than follow a straight line. The resulting line is called the fitted curve.
The derivative is the slope of that fitted curve: how quickly the fitted outcome changes for each additional hour of photoperiod at each point. Here it is evaluated on the model’s linear-predictor scale, in model-scale units per hour; the left-hand fitted curves are displayed in the named metric units.
A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes uncertainty at one photoperiod value. It is not a simultaneous uncertainty band for the whole curve.

Overlap among nonlinear model terms can make their separate contributions harder to distinguish. This is reported below using the technical term concurvity.

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure
section: Nonlinear photoperiod model and qualifying-transition rule
text:
Nonlinear photoperiod model and qualifying-transition rule
Each metric and placement used a separate nonlinear GAM fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. The reported model was:
Show R codeformula_registry |>
  filter(.data$model_id == "adapted_photoperiod_smooth") |>
  pull(.data$formula) |>
  cat()
response_value ~ s(photoperiod_hours, k = 6, bs = “tp”) + s(site, bs = “re”) + s(site_participant, bs = “re”)
Here, response_value is the response shown in the specification table, photoperiod_hours is civil photoperiod, site is the study site, and site_participant identifies a participant within site. The smooth used a thin-plate regression spline with basis dimension k = 6. A broader k = 10 smooth and a model treating site as a fixed effect were fitted as model-form sensitivities.
Absolute latitude is fixed within site. It is therefore structurally confounded with site, and a latitude-by-photoperiod surface cannot separately identify a latitude association while accounting for site. The planned joint surface was inspected as an identifiability check but is not used for inference or for the qualifying-transition classification. No temperature or other unplanned environmental predictor was added.
For each reported smooth, the first derivative was evaluated at 100 equally spaced values over that metric’s exact recorded photoperiod range. Central finite differences used a step of 0.01 h, with one-sided differences at the two boundaries. Unconditional model-coefficient covariance produced pointwise 95% confidence intervals on the model’s linear-predictor scale.
A qualifying transition from increase to a sustained near-flat tail1 required all three conditions:

the immediately preceding grid point had a derivative interval wholly above zero;
the next grid point had a derivative interval containing zero; and
every later grid point through the longest recorded photoperiod also had a zero-compatible derivative interval.

The reported transition is the bracket from the last pointwise detected increase to the first point of the sustained zero-compatible tail. This is the requested change from a statistically supported positive derivative to a non-significant derivative that remains non-significant to the end of the recorded range. The rule does not define a scientifically negligible slope, prove equivalence to zero, locate a true asymptote, or demonstrate a mechanism. The 100 pointwise checks and the nine cross-metric classifications were not multiplicity-adjusted; the classification is therefore descriptive.

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure
text:
Interpretation and limitations
The pooled analysis shows several fitted photoperiod associations that rise and then meet the prespecified pointwise rule for a sustained zero-compatible derivative. The recurring patterns for mean melEDI, darkest 10 h mean, both above-threshold duration metrics, and melEDI dose across the two placements are the most consistent descriptive findings. Brightest 10 h mean differs by placement, the longest-period result is sensitive to sample definition and model form, and the chest sleep low-light result is undermined by distributional failure, common-row analyses, model-form changes, and site influence.
The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore that qualifying transitions from increase to a sustained near-flat tail are visible for several personal light-exposure metrics in the pooled data, subject to substantial design and model limitations. The results do not establish a ceiling, an equivalence region, a causal effect of photoperiod, a distinct latitude effect, a health or clinical consequence, or equivalence between near-eye and chest placement.

text:
Preregistration deviations


DEV-016: the registered latitude-by-photoperiod surface is non-identifiable here, so the accepted report retains all nine outcomes and presents a separately labelled site-adjusted nonlinear photoperiod analysis as descriptive evidence.

DEV-033: all nine eligible outcomes remain visible rather than being selected using H01 significance or H07 AIC.

DEV-034: response specifications and model checks are metric-specific rather than one universal zero-aware log-Gaussian model.

title: H07 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
Temporal order and repeated participant-days
Dates are local calendar dates. Civil photoperiod is joined by site and local date. Frames are ordered by site, participant, and date before fitting. Participants contribute repeated days, so each model contains a random-effect smooth for participant nested within site. Site also has its own random-effect smooth. One participant-day contributes only one row per metric and placement; there is no within-day residual time series in H07.
No independent temperature, season, or collection-period predictor is added. Season and collection period remain embedded in the observed date and photoperiod pattern. Consecutive-day residual correlations are descriptive checks of remaining temporal dependence rather than a fitted autocorrelation structure.

Association and derivative estimands
The association estimand is the fitted pooled civil-photoperiod smooth for one metric and placement, conditional on the model structure. Response-scale curves are used for scientific display: when a response was transformed for fitting, the fitted quantity was converted back to the displayed metric unit. The derivative estimand underlying the qualifying transition is the first derivative of that smooth on the model’s linear-predictor scale per hour of civil photoperiod.
For each metric and placement, derivatives are evaluated at 100 equally spaced points from the exact minimum to maximum recorded photoperiod. Central finite differences use an increment of 0.01 h; the lower boundary uses a forward difference and the upper boundary a backward difference. The pointwise 95% interval uses the unconditional covariance matrix.
A pattern is present only when:

the immediately preceding grid point has a derivative interval wholly above zero;
the next point has a derivative interval containing zero; and
every later point through the recorded maximum also has an interval containing zero.

The transition is bracketed by the preceding and current grid points. A non-significant derivative at one point, a visual flattening, or an AIC threshold is not sufficient. The rule has no scientifically defensible equivalence margin, no simultaneous curve band, and no curve-wide or cross-metric multiplicity adjustment. It therefore supports only a pointwise, descriptive qualifying-transition classification, not a ceiling claim.

text:
Model checks and support limits
All 18 reported photoperiod-smooth fits converged. Four smooths—three near-eye and one chest—met the recorded basis-dimension flag criterion, motivating the broader-basis sensitivity. Estimated overlap among nonlinear model terms (concurvity) supplied by the nested participant smooth to the photoperiod smooth was approximately 0.9985–0.9988. This is the principal identifiability limitation: the pooled photoperiod shape is difficult to separate from which participants contribute at which photoperiods.

Residual summaries retained fitted-value dependence and tail checks for every metric. Residual autocorrelation means that observations close in sequence retain more similar residuals than observations farther apart. text:
Sensitivity analyses and site influence
Candidate samples
Each sensitivity changes a named feature. The gap-timing-unaware dataset omits the additional metric-specific adjustment based on when remaining gaps occur while retaining the coverage rules. The paired/common analysis keeps only participant-days available at both sensor positions. The cross-dataset common-row analyses restrict the primary and gap-timing-unaware definitions to identical rows. The longest-period analysis keeps only days with an exactly identified period, and the dose analysis compares observed and corrected melEDI dose on identical rows. Model-form sensitivities increase photoperiod-smooth flexibility from k = 6 to k = 10 or represent site with fixed rather than random effects. title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
text:
The Visual Light Sensitivity Questionnaire (VLSQ-8) measures self-reported visual light sensitivity; higher scores indicate greater sensitivity according to the accepted scale.
The preregistered hypothesis was:

H8: Duration-, exposure-history-, and level-based metrics are associated with VLSQ-8 light sensitivity scores.

The analytical question is whether VLSQ-8 is associated with repeated participant-day personal light-exposure metrics after adjustment for study site. A participant-day is one participant’s eligible local calendar day. The primary near-eye sensor position more closely represents light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is not an ocular-exposure measure and is not pooled with near-eye measurements. Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) describes light in terms of melanopsin-weighted visual-system sensitivity.
Reported effects compare VLSQ-8 scores separated by one participant-level standard deviation (SD), equal to 5.540 points. Time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep is reported as an absolute difference in hours; the eight log-link outcomes are reported as ratios and corresponding percentage changes, on a separate scale. A back-transformed estimate returns a fitted coefficient to its stated hour-difference, ratio, or percentage-change scale. A 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes the uncertainty around that effect; Wald construction is named where relevant.
The site-average association is an average across sites that gives each site equal weight. The separate VLSQ-8-by-site interaction allows the association between VLSQ-8 and a light metric to differ by study site. False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment is applied within each declared nine-metric family.






NoteAnswer in brief



Across nine light-exposure metrics, neither the primary near-eye site-average associations nor their VLSQ-8-by-site interactions met the FDR-adjusted criterion. The strongest near-eye directional pattern was lower corrected melEDI dose per VLSQ-8 SD (ratio 0.846, 95% CI 0.716–0.999; raw p = 0.051, FDR-adjusted p = 0.160), so it is not an FDR-retained finding. Complementary chest results and the central sensitivity analyses did not change that conclusion, although site influence and specified model limitations require caution.

title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure
section: Score, sensor positions, and light-exposure metrics
text:
Score, sensor positions, and light-exposure metrics
VLSQ-8 was available for all 184 participants across nine sites. The stored score equalled the sum of eight ordered 1–5 item codes plus 5 for every participant. Scores ranged from 13 to 39, with a mean of 21.598 and a participant SD of 5.540. The raw score was centred at the observed mean; no within-site standardisation was used.
Nine participant-day outcomes covered light level, duration, continuous periods, and exposure history. All use manuscript metric names and melEDI units. Current definitions are documented in Preparation 04, and the model-ready inputs in Preparation 06. The longest continuous period is an observed lower bound unless its start and end are both exactly identified; that stricter definition is examined as a sensitivity analysis.
The predefined preparation sensitivity is called the gap-timing-unaware dataset. It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. The name means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment; it does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored. For this one-time first explanation, the primary could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset because its approved preparation uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant. From here onward, it is called simply the primary dataset.

Render boundary
Rendering this page recalculates only file-identity checks, schema and key checks, and lightweight descriptive summaries from frozen H08 model frames. The two near-eye last-timing slopes were close to zero and changed direction under some participant-deletion and leave-one-site-out checks, although no deletion changed a slope by the material 0.25-hour threshold. Chest longest-period/MEQ had a singular maximum-likelihood chronotype-by-site interaction fit; its additive main-effect fit remained estimable, but that interaction fit remains a model-check limitation. The registered longest-period outcome was unavailable in the gap-timing-unaware prepared artifact at both placements and for both instruments. Fixed-effect matrices were full rank and Hessians positive definite for all stored fits. Repeated observations closer in time may retain more similar residuals, a dependence called autocorrelation. A continuous-time first-order autoregressive, or AR(1), sensitivity represented this dependence as stronger at shorter elapsed-time gaps; its corrections changed slopes by at most 0.016 h.

title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure
text:
Other named sensitivity analyses
The photoperiod sensitivity added centered within-site photoperiod to the participant-day model. It was stable for 21 of 24 targets; its two direction-sensitive results were the near-zero near-eye last-timing slopes, and one chest mean-timing estimate was precision-sensitive. The participant summary sensitivity replaced repeated participant-day outcomes with one equal-weight outcome mean per participant; it was stable for 20 of 24 targets, with direction changes confined to near-zero last-timing or chest longest-period slopes. All 24 continuous-time AR(1) checks of residual autocorrelation were stable. The L10 clock-cut sensitivity compared the registered strict >16:00 negative-hour conversion with a noon cut; slopes changed by at most 0.037 h, and all four checks were acceptable.

title: H09 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
This page explains how verified chronotype fields and personal light-exposure timing metrics lead to the scientific findings in the H09 results report.
H09 asks whether participant-level chronotype is associated with five participant-day timing metrics of personal light exposure. A participant-day is one participant’s eligible outcome on one local date. Chronotype is represented by the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire corrected midsleep on free days (MCTQ MSFsc) and the Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). Larger MCTQ MSFsc means later corrected midsleep, whereas larger MEQ means greater morning preference; the two constructs remain separate in the models and inferential families.
Personal light exposure is expressed as melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI). The primary near-eye sensor position records light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is analysed separately, is not pooled with near-eye measurement, and is not a measure of ocular exposure.
The gap-timing-unaware dataset is the dataset applying the 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules but not using the remaining gaps’ time of day in metric-specific support decisions. At this first explanation it can be contrasted with the time-sensitive primary dataset; hereafter the latter is called simply the primary dataset.
This page identifies the exact inputs, derived fields, analytical frames, formulae, model checks, sensitivity analyses, outputs, and file identities behind the results. It documents provenance and does not create an additional analysis. Uncertainty is reported as 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs), and multiplicity is handled with false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment.

title: H09 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
This page explains how verified chronotype fields and personal light-exposure timing metrics lead to the scientific findings in the H09 results report.
H09 asks whether participant-level chronotype is associated with five participant-day timing metrics of personal light exposure. A participant-day is one participant’s eligible outcome on one local date. Chronotype is represented by the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire corrected midsleep on free days (MCTQ MSFsc) and the Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). Larger MCTQ MSFsc means later corrected midsleep, whereas larger MEQ means greater morning preference; the two constructs remain separate in the models and inferential families.
Personal light exposure is expressed as melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI). The primary near-eye sensor position records light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is analysed separately, is not pooled with near-eye measurement, and is not a measure of ocular exposure.
The gap-timing-unaware dataset is the dataset applying the 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules but not using the remaining gaps’ time of day in metric-specific support decisions. At this first explanation it can be contrasted with the time-sensitive primary dataset; hereafter the latter is called simply the primary dataset.
This page identifies the exact inputs, derived fields, analytical frames, formulae, model checks, sensitivity analyses, outputs, and file identities behind the results. It documents provenance and does not create an additional analysis. Uncertainty is reported as 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs), and multiplicity is handled with false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment.

Centering and scaling
The two model-column names, mctq_hour_centered and meq_10_centered, encode only a change of origin and, for MEQ, a reporting scale:


MCTQ: mctq_hour_centered = MCTQ MSFsc in hours - 4.1135843

Thus one MCTQ unit means one hour later corrected midsleep, while one MEQ unit means 10 score points toward greater morning preference. A centered value of zero is the observed participant mean. Centering changes the intercept’s reference point; it does not change the chronotype slope, its 95% CI, or its test.

Timing metrics and analytical samples
Metric definitions
Five registered participant-day outcomes enter each confirmatory family: the midpoint of the brightest 10 hours (M10 midpoint), midpoint of the darkest 10 hours (L10 midpoint), first and last time above 250 lx melEDI, and midpoint of the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI. The longest-period midpoint is calculated only when the selected period is exactly identifiable from its recorded endpoints. Mean timing above 250 lx melEDI is a distinct sensitivity estimand and is not substituted for the registered midpoint. M10 and L10 onset and offset are excluded. Preparation 04 documents metric derivation, and Preparation 06 documents the model-ready fields and support.
Clock values were linearized because their observed support was adequately linear. Night-time values use the specified negative-hour conversion where applicable; no circular response distribution was imposed merely because an outcome is clock-valued.

title: H09 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
Models, estimands, uncertainty, and multiplicity
Exact formulae supplied to the models
For each metric, placement, dataset, sample, and chronotype instrument, the site-only model is compared with an additive chronotype model. The additive model estimates the study-site-adjusted average association and includes a participant random effect, which represents remaining between-participant timing variation after site and chronotype are considered. A second comparison adds a chronotype-by-site interaction, allowing the chronotype association to differ by study site. The distinction between these two questions is recorded in DEV-038.
Each coefficient is a signed effect in local clock hours. Positive values mean the timing outcome occurs later per one-hour later MCTQ MSFsc or per 10 points greater MEQ morning preference; negative values mean earlier. Restricted maximum-likelihood additive fits provide coefficients and 95% Wald CIs; maximum-likelihood fits provide the nested likelihood-ratio tests. A natural-spline fit is used only to assess whether the observed predictor support is adequately represented as linear.

title: H09 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
Model checks, influence, and limitations
Sixteen model-check domains (model diagnostics) were interpreted for each of 24 primary metric-by-instrument-by-placement targets. Stored checks cover questionnaire provenance, sample and join identity, site support, clock representation, linearity, residual distribution and spread, convergence, singularity, rank, temporal dependence, participant and site influence, placement identity, preparation sensitivity, and multiplicity.
Visual inspection of the complete residual panels supported acceptable final response/residual distribution and heteroscedasticity assessments. The quantitative screen values remain stored. Eighteen targets are acceptable across all domains; six retain an influence, interaction-fit, or unavailable preparation-sensitivity limitation.

The retained limitations among those six targets have specific interpretations. The two near-eye last-timing slopes were close to zero and changed direction under some participant-deletion and leave-one-site-out checks, although no deletion changed a slope by the material 0.25-hour threshold. The chest longest-period/MEQ maximum-likelihood chronotype-by-site interaction fit was singular; its additive average-association fit remained estimable. Fixed-effect matrices were full rank and Hessians positive definite for all stored fits.
The complete model-check registry, screen-to-final assessment record, participant-influence summary, and leave-one-site-out summary preserve the values and assessment basis. No model-check flag automatically removes an observation.

  all(accepted_reader_transitions$status == "FAIL"),
  all(nchar(accepted_reader_transitions$sha256) == 64L),
  all(nchar(accepted_reader_transitions$current_sha256) == 64L)
)
expected_historical_paths <- accepted_reader_transitions$path
immutable_reader_manifest <- reader_manifest |>
  filter(!.data$path %in% mutable_records)
manifest_paths <- file.path(root, immutable_reader_manifest$path)
manifest_exists <- file.exists(manifest_paths)
manifest_current_sha <- rep(NA_character_, length(manifest_paths))
manifest_current_bytes <- rep(NA_real_, length(manifest_paths))
manifest_current_sha[manifest_exists] <- vapply(
  manifest_paths[manifest_exists],
  artifact_sha256,
  character(1)
)
manifest_current_bytes[manifest_exists] <- unname(
  file.info(manifest_paths[manifest_exists])$size
)
manifest_audit <- immutable_reader_manifest |>
  mutate(
    path_exists = manifest_exists,
    current_sha256 = manifest_current_sha,
    current_bytes = manifest_current_bytes,
    live_exact = .data$path_exists &
      .data$current_sha256 == .data$sha256 &
      .data$current_bytes == as.numeric(.data$bytes)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    accepted_reader_transitions |>
      transmute(
        path = .data$path,
        accepted_historical_sha256 = .data$sha256,
        accepted_historical_bytes = as.numeric(.data$bytes),
        accepted_live_sha256 = .data$current_sha256,
        accepted_live_bytes = as.numeric(.data$current_bytes)
      ),
    by = "path",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    accepted_transition = !.data$live_exact &
      .data$path %in% expected_historical_paths &
      .data$sha256 == .data$accepted_historical_sha256 &
      as.numeric(.data$bytes) == .data$accepted_historical_bytes &
      .data$current_sha256 == .data$accepted_live_sha256 &
      .data$current_bytes == .data$accepted_live_bytes,
    Status = case_when(
      .data$live_exact ~ "LIVE_EXACT",
      .data$accepted_transition ~ "ACCEPTED_HISTORICAL_TO_LIVE",
      TRUE ~ "FAIL"
    )
  )
observed_historical_paths <- manifest_audit |>
  filter(!.data$live_exact) |>
  pull(.data$path)
stopifnot(
  nrow(reader_manifest) == 108L,
  nrow(immutable_reader_manifest) == 106L,
  all(manifest_audit$path_exists),
  sum(manifest_audit$Status == "LIVE_EXACT") == 87L,
  sum(manifest_audit$Status == "ACCEPTED_HISTORICAL_TO_LIVE") == 19L,
  !any(manifest_audit$Status == "FAIL"),
  identical(sort(observed_historical_paths), sort(expected_historical_paths))
)
manifest_check <- tibble::tibble(
  Check = c(
    "Immutable manifest paths exist",
    "Live-exact identities",
    "Accepted historical-to-live transitions",
    "Exact historical path set",
    "Manifest rows are unique",
    "Recorded R version"
  ),
  Observed = c(
    paste0(sum(manifest_audit$path_exists), " / " , nrow(manifest_audit)),
    paste0(sum(manifest_audit$Status == "LIVE_EXACT"), " / 87"),
    paste0(
      sum(manifest_audit$Status == "ACCEPTED_HISTORICAL_TO_LIVE"),
      " / 19"
    ),
    paste0(length(observed_historical_paths), " / 19"),
    paste0(nrow(reader_manifest), " / 108"),
    paste(sort(unique(reader_manifest$r_version)), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  Status = c(
    if_else(all(manifest_audit$path_exists), "PASS", "FAIL"),
    if_else(
      sum(manifest_audit$Status == "LIVE_EXACT") == 87L,
      "PASS",
      "FAIL"
    ),
    if_else(
      sum(manifest_audit$Status == "ACCEPTED_HISTORICAL_TO_LIVE") == 19L,
      "PASS",
      "FAIL"
    ),
    if_else(
      identical(sort(observed_historical_paths), sort(expected_historical_paths)),
      "PASS",
      "FAIL"
    ),
    if_else(!anyDuplicated(reader_manifest$path), "PASS", "FAIL"),
    if_else(all(reader_manifest$r_version == "4.6.1"), "PASS", "FAIL")
  )
)
stopifnot(all(manifest_check$Status == "PASS"))

Core residual checks
The assessment above is complemented by the standard residual-versus-fitted and normal Q-Q displays below. They show every main-association model that met its separately labelled 17-metric FDR rule: nine age models and two measured- biological-sex models. Each panel has its own limits because fitted scales and residual ranges differ across metrics. Points use submitted site colours so site-specific clustering or tail behaviour remains visible.

The age display has paired source data.







Figure 6: Residual-versus-fitted and descriptive normal Q-Q plots for the two complementary chest biological-sex models that met their separately labelled 17-metric FDR rule. Panels use independent limits; point colours follow submitted site conventions.




The biological-sex display has paired source data. A 68-page diagnostic appendix provides the same two plots for every primary metric-sensor-position-association model, with an exact page and assessment index and complete plot data.
The Q-Q panels are descriptive checks of stored Pearson residuals, including for Tweedie responses; they are not separate normality tests and do not replace the family-specific distribution, zero-mass, temporal, convergence, or influence assessments. The plots make the recorded tail and spread qualifications visible but do not change any model’s acceptability assessment.

title: H10: Age, measured biological sex, and personal light exposure
text:
Sensor-position-matched analysis
This sensitivity analysis used the same participants and participant-days at both sensor positions for each of the 15 participant-day metrics. Near-eye and chest associations were fitted separately, so this is neither an equivalence test nor a direct sensor-position effect test. All key identities matched. Participant-level IS and IV were unavailable for this comparison because no approved artifact recomputes them on identical paired participant-day sets; they were not approximated.







Figure 7: Sensor-position-matched estimates from separate near-eye and chest models; the identity line is descriptive and is not an equivalence margin.




On matched participant-days, near-eye time above 1,000 lx melEDI retained adjusted support for age; brightest-10-hour mean and melEDI dose retained positive directions but not adjusted support. All eight complementary chest main findings retained their directions and adjusted support. The paired analysis additionally supported chest pre-sleep time below 10 lx melEDI for age and chest brightest-10-hour mean for measured biological sex; these remain sensitivity-only findings.
The display has paired source data, and the complete paired estimates, 95% CIs, exact samples, and p-values are available here.

title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance
section: Verified inputs, demographic construct, and response contracts
text:
Verified inputs, demographic construct, and response contracts
Verified inputs and current qualification
The analysis used the current Preparation 06 model-ready layer. Its base objects contained 816 near-eye and 902 chest participant-days before metric-specific availability was applied. The model-ready layer, current MDER values, and L10 numerical-zero normalization were independently verified. The L10 normalization changed exactly eight primary L10 values from numerical noise to exact zero without changing a sample, a non-L10 scientific value, or an inferential decision. The corrected gap-timing-unaware chest day with no viable momentary ratio is recorded as missing, and every finite gap MDER value is strictly positive.
The remaining qualification is explicit: complete independent reconstruction of the exact current state-support classification remains open. This qualification is not evidence that the stored values are incorrect.
Demographic construct and site support
Age and biological sex were joined as participant-level variables and were complete in every fitted frame. Biological sex had exactly the levels Male and Female. Male was the reference, so the reported coefficient is Female minus Male. Site was explicitly sum-coded. The gender variable and unsupported predictors did not enter any model.
The smallest fitted site-by-sex cell was the near-eye San José (CR) Male cell with two participants. This was estimable but motivated the interaction and leave-one-site-out qualifications.

For METRIC-010, daily MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios on a complete 1,440-minute local wall-clock grid. A minute is viable only when both channels are finite and strictly positive, and the daily value is retained with at least 720 viable minutes. Fall-back duplicate local minutes are averaged channel-wise before forming the ratio; spring-forward absent minutes remain missing. The analysis does not use time-profile weighting or a ratio of daily integrals.

Rows with missing outcome, age, biological sex, site or participant identifier were excluded before the frame was indexed. Every stored row had a unique key that included dataset, placement, metric, site, participant, and participant or date unit.

All converged; positive-definite Hessians; full-rank fixed effects; no singular fit or fit error.


Residual and distributional checks
68 primary targets
Residual spread, Q–Q correlation, fitted-response bounds, dispersion, and zero-mass evidence were interpreted jointly.


Temporal dependence
37,576 consecutive-day residual pairs
All 60 participant-day checks passed the descriptive threshold; maximum absolute correlation 0.239.


Participant deletion
68 target summaries
Every check passed; maximum change 0.319 full-fit standard errors.


Leave one site out
68 target summaries
No failed refit; maximum change 1.72 full-fit standard errors.


Final classification
25 acceptable; 43 acceptable with specified limitations
No primary target was classified not acceptable.









The most recurrent qualifications were residual-spread or Q–Q flags for selected right-skewed or timing responses, plus a zero-mass mismatch for sleep- environment time below 1 lx melEDI. Four observed zeros at each sensor position remained in those fitted Tweedie models. These issues were retained in the interpretation rather than used to select an unregistered replacement model.
Complete numerical model-check results are available in the assessment file, participant-deletion, and leave-one-site-out files.
The results report also displays residual-versus-fitted and descriptive normal Q-Q plots for all 11 multiplicity-retained main-association models. A 68-page appendix provides the same core plots for all 68 primary models, with an exact page and assessment index and complete plot data. These displays are constructed from the stored fitted values, Pearson residuals, and Q-Q points already produced by the analysis; no model is refitted and no assessment is recalculated.

Sensitivity analyses
Each sensitivity analysis changed one declared feature while retaining the H10 estimand and model implementation. The gap-timing-unaware dataset applies the same general coverage rules as the primary dataset but does not use the timing of remaining missing observations for metric-specific adjustment. The sensitivity analyses were not used to replace the primary conclusion.

section: Can the global results be separated into level and shape?
text:
Can the global results be separated into level and shape?
These secondary attribution tests are subordinate to the complete-curve tests in Table 2. They ask whether each globally supported curve can be assigned cleanly to an independently supported level or shape component.

Within each placement and dataset, level and shape form a two-test false-discovery-rate family. Raw and adjusted p-values are labelled and bolded independently at their respective p < 0.050 rules. These secondary tests ask whether the globally tested curve can be resolved into an independently supported level or shape component; they do not retest or invalidate the separate global curve result.








The secondary attribution did not cleanly resolve the globally supported curve into an independently supported level or shape component. The shape component had raw p = 0.043 but FDR-adjusted p = 0.075; the level component had raw and adjusted p = 0.075. The global result is not formed by adding or combining these two p-values. Evidence can be distributed across correlated level and shape directions, so this result expresses uncertainty about attribution and does not make the global result invalid.

The chest global result is visually level-like, but the secondary attribution did not resolve that result independently to the level term: its raw p = 0.029 and FDR-adjusted p = 0.057. The shape component had raw and adjusted p = 0.986. This limits component attribution and does not overturn the separately supported complete-curve result.
Why there is no direct placement identity plot
The all-available near-eye and chest models use different samples, so plotting their estimates against one another would confound placement with sample composition. A stored common frame contains 112 participants, 643 participant- days, 29,786 matched observations, and eight sites, but no accepted H11 model was fitted to that frame and no scalar temporal estimand was predeclared. Therefore a matched identity scatterplot is not applicable. The separate near-eye and chest curves above are the closest valid comparison; they do not test placement differences or establish equivalence.

Participant share is the largest contribution to the unscaled participant-cluster covariance meat trace. Effective participants is the corresponding trace-based concentration summary.








All four models are acceptable with specified limitations. They converged without serious fitting warnings; the cyclic sex curves close at midnight; site deviations satisfy their sum-to-zero constraint; and no severe basis- dimension flag was found. The accepted AR structure reduced boundary-aware lag-1 residual correlation from approximately 0.60–0.62 before adjustment to 0.070–0.083 in the final residuals.


Near eye
