Figure 6: Boundary-aware near-eye residual autocorrelation before and after the accepted AR(1) adjustment. Correlations use only pairs within valid participant-day sequences.













Figure 7: Boundary-aware chest residual autocorrelation before and after the accepted AR(1) adjustment. Correlations use only pairs within valid participant-day sequences.














Figure 8: Residual-distribution and scale diagnostics for the primary near-eye and complementary chest models. Panel A shows stored final standardized-residual quantiles overall and by recorded biological sex: thin lines span the 1st–99th percentiles, medium lines the 5th–95th percentiles, thick lines the interquartile range, and points the median. Panel B shows the stored correlation between absolute residual magnitude and the fitted value. Medians are close to zero, while broad tails and positive correlations of 0.197–0.240 show remaining heavy tails and heteroscedasticity.




Residual-distribution diagnostic source data
Together, the residual figures show the main continuous diagnostic outcomes: the accepted AR(1) structure removes most short-lag dependence, while the final residuals remain centered near zero but retain heavy tails and fitted-value-dependent spread. Convergence, cyclic closure, the site constraint, and basis-dimension flags remain in the diagnostic table because they are pass/fail or count outcomes rather than quantities that benefit from a separate plot.
No single participant dominates the robust covariance: the largest participant contribution is 2.8–3.0% near eye and 7.5–7.6% at chest. The coefficient-held-fixed delete-one-participant covariance check retains the global decision for every participant. This check probes covariance influence; it is not a leave-one-participant-out model-refit sensitivity.
The remaining limitations are material but do not invalidate the specified test. Exact zeros, heavy tails, heteroscedasticity, and concurvity remain under the Gaussian log-scale mean model. Results are conditional on the observed sites; the site sample is too small for broad site-population generalisation, and leave-one-site-out refits remain unresolved. The registered hourly geometric-mean outcome remains the documented preregistered specification but is outside the accepted H11 analysis rather than an outstanding sensitivity. A fitted common-placement sample, an all-zero-inclusive preparation, and alternative temporal model forms remain unresolved. The activity-context sensitivity is now reported, but it is limited to uniquely mapped single- activity diary hours and cannot distinguish covariate adjustment from selection into the activity-complete sample without the explicit same-sample comparison shown above.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns
text:
Preregistration deviations
The analysis differs from, or makes operationally explicit, the preregistered plan in the following ways. The registered hourly geometric-mean outcome remains preregistration provenance but is outside and superseded by the author-approved final H11 analysis. It is not an outstanding or unresolved sensitivity.



Table 14: H11 data, placement, and estimand deviations or clarifications.













Preregistered
Analysed
Consequence



Outcome and epoch
Hourly geometric-mean melEDI
Thirty-minute arithmetic-mean melEDI, transformed as log10(melEDI + 0.1)
The accepted H11 estimand, row count, scale, and dependence structure follow the author-approved H02 adaptation and therefore differ from preregistration; the registered hourly outcome remains the documented preregistered specification, not an outstanding H11 sensitivity.


Placement role
Chest primary; near eye as robustness placement
Near eye primary; chest complementary
The measurement closer to the eye carries the primary interpretation.


Day inclusion
Coverage-based exclusions; no deletion solely because a binned profile is constant
Inherited coverage rules plus upstream exclusion of otherwise eligible verified exact-all-zero device days; supported constant profiles retained
The fitted samples reconcile to the accepted temporal-analysis samples.


Analysis hierarchy
Repeated hourly observations with participant and site effects
Thirty-minute observations nested in participant-day and participant, conditional on observed sites
Participant-specific curves and participant-day intercepts change weighting and uncertainty.












Table 15: H11 model, inference, and reporting deviations or clarifications.













Preregistered
Analysed
Consequence



Sex and time terms
Parametric sex effect plus cyclic sex-specific time smooth
Parametric Female level plus cyclic Female-minus-Male deviation; common daily curve retained
The joint null covers both a time-constant level and a time-varying shape difference.


Site and participant structure
Site factor smooth, site random effect, and participant random-effect smooth
Inherited sum-to-zero site temporal deviations, participant-specific time curves, and participant-day random intercept; no site random intercept
Inference is conditional on these observed sites and the richer repeated-measure structure.


Additional context
No photoperiod-state or activity-adjusted causal estimand
No photoperiod-state term or activity adjustment in the accepted test; an exploratory same-sample activity-context adjustment was added
Sample restriction and observational adjustment are shown separately; no behavioural, causal, or mediational interpretation is made.


Inference and multiplicity
Delta AIC of at least 2; AR(1) if needed; FDR if multiple tests
Participant-cluster robust global curve test; separate two-test BH level/shape decomposition
The confirmatory claim is the complete curve, not a selected pointwise interval or raw component p-value.

Source data and technical provenance
The scientific preparation, model construction, and provenance checks are documented in the H11 analysis preparation and provenance.
Exact full-precision reader sources are available for the fitted samples, global tests, level and shape decomposition, effect-size summaries, sex-specific curves, Female-minus-Male contrasts, activity-context samples, activity-context global comparisons, activity-context pointwise contrasts, accepted-model diagnostics, residual-distribution diagnostics, and activity-context diagnostics.

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
This page explains how the verified H02 temporal frames and recorded biological sex were turned into the inference presented in the H11 results report.
H11 asks whether the 24-hour pattern of personal melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) differs by the biological-sex variable recorded in the study. Biological sex and gender identity are distinct constructs; gender identity was not analysed. The near-eye sensor position is primary. The chest sensor position provides complementary evidence and is not a measure of ocular exposure. This placement change is recorded in DEV-001.
The reported estimand is the complete Female-minus-Male fitted curve across 48 half-hour clock bins, averaged equally across included sites and conditional on the fitted temporal, participant, participant-day, site, and autocorrelation structure. A site-average fitted mean averages across included sites and gives each site equal weight. The participant is the independent unit for robust inference. A participant-day is one participant’s included observations on one local calendar day; model rows are 30-minute observations nested within participant-days and participants.
The accepted preregistration differences are consolidated in the H11 preregistration-deviations section.

Temporal and analytical-frame construction
Inherited time structure
H11 inherits the finalized temporal architecture documented in the H02 analysis preparation and provenance rather than selecting a new one. Local wall-clock time is represented by 48 half-hour midpoints from 00:15 to 23:45. The smooth is cyclic, meaning that it joins smoothly across midnight. Site-specific time patterns sum to zero, participant-specific time curves represent remaining within-participant variation, and participant-day random effects represent remaining variation within local calendar days. The hierarchy and site structure are recorded in DEV-044 and DEV-045.
Autocorrelation sequences are based on true elapsed instants. A sequence restarts at participant-day boundaries, elapsed-time discontinuities, and non-one-to-one wall-clock outcomes, including daylight-saving-time ambiguity. The accepted frames therefore do not infer continuity merely because two rows have adjacent clock labels.

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
2. Nonlinear GAM construction
A nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) allows the daily melEDI pattern to vary smoothly and nonlinearly over clock time. Cyclic smooths join smoothly across midnight. Participant-specific time curves and participant-day random effects represent remaining repeated-measure variation after the shared time, biological-sex, and site structure is considered. Autocorrelation is residual similarity between observations close together in time; an AR(1) structure represents this similarity as stronger at shorter lags.
Exact Wilkinson formulas
The following are the exact formulas supplied to the accepted model fits. The cells are displayed for auditability and are not executed on this page.

Show the R code used for this displayM_pattern <- response ~ sex +
  s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, by = sex_smooth, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +
  s(participant_day, bs = "re")



Show the R code used for this displayM_0 <- response ~
  s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +
  s(participant_day, bs = "re")



Show the R code used for this displayM_activity <- response ~ sex + activity +
  s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, by = sex_smooth, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, by = activity_smooth, bs = "cc", k = 12, id = 2) +
  s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +
  s(participant_day, bs = "re")



Show the R code used for this displayM_activity_0 <- response ~ activity +
  s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, by = activity_smooth, bs = "cc", k = 12, id = 2) +
  s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) +
  s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) +
  s(participant_day, bs = "re")


The sex factor uses Male as the treatment-reference level. The ordered sex_smooth factor identifies the cyclic Female-minus-Male deviation. The main cyclic smooth is the Male reference curve; the sex-deviation smooth adds the Female shape difference. Site deviations use the sum-to-zero basis, participant curves use factor smooths, and participant-day random intercepts account for repeated observations within days. In the activity model, Home is the treatment reference and the ordered activity deviation smooths share one smoothing parameter (id = 2).
The biological-sex/time specification is recorded in DEV-043, and the site and participant structure is recorded in DEV-044 and DEV-045.

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
3. Estimand, uncertainty, and multiplicity
Complete-curve inference
The complete-curve, or global, test is one joint test of the time-constant and time-varying Female-minus-Male contributions across the whole 48-bin, 24-hour curve within each placement and dataset. Inference uses participant-summed, AR-whitened scores; a participant-cluster CR1 covariance; the smoothing-bias term V_p-V_e; and a finite-cluster, fractional-rank F reference. A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) applies to one displayed clock bin. It is not a simultaneous band across the full day. All displayed curve, contrast, and scalar intervals are pointwise 95% CIs.
The primary near-eye global raw p-value is 0.028 and the complementary chest raw p-value is 0.029. Each is the sole member of its explicitly labelled global family, so its stored adjusted value is numerically identical. FDR adjustment is applied within separately labelled families. This complete-curve inference and multiplicity specification is recorded in DEV-048.

What the two-component decomposition can and cannot say
The complete-curve result is the overall test. A separate, secondary decomposition asks whether that curve difference can be attributed cleanly to (1) a constant parametric level component or (2) a cyclic shape component. Those two attribution tests form a two-test FDR family within each placement and dataset.
No component remains supported after that two-test adjustment. This does not invalidate or reverse the significant global curve result. It means only that the evidence cannot cleanly separate the overall curve association into an independent “level” contribution and an independent “shape” contribution after accounting for the two attribution attempts. The two components are parameterization-dependent parts of one fitted curve and are not a second omnibus test of whether the full curve differs.

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance
text:
5. Sensitivity analyses and deferred comparisons
Gap timing
The gap-timing-unaware dataset still passed the general requirement for at least 50% valid data per hour and at least 80% valid data per participant-day. “Gap-timing-unaware” means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for metric-specific adjustment. For contrast only in this first explanation, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset; hereafter it is called simply the primary dataset.
Applying the same model and global test to the gap-timing-unaware dataset gave raw global p-values of 0.026 near eye and 0.037 at chest. This supports stability to whether the timing of remaining missing observations is used for metric-specific adjustment. It does not test every possible missing-data mechanism.
Activity context
The exploratory activity analysis uses the accepted primary placement frames and a normalized hourly diary. A 30-minute observation is retained only when there is exactly one containing diary hour and exactly one eligible mapped activity: Home, Sleep, Public transport/car, Indoor work/home office, or Outdoors/active travel. Missing flags, no selection, multiple selections, and an unspecified “other” selection are not imputed. Autocorrelation sequences restart across gaps created by this filter.

All models are Gaussian identity-link additive models fitted by fast REML with discrete = TRUE and cyclic knots time_hour = c(0, 24). title: Planned sensitivity checks
text:
Manuscript-prepared-data sensitivity
Every hypothesis receives a manuscript-prepared-data sensitivity. The same new H01–H11 code and models are fitted twice: once to the newly prepared data for the main analysis and once to the dataset prepared for the manuscript, with only objectively demonstrable data errors corrected. This comparison therefore isolates the effect of data preparation and metric calculation.
It does not rerun the manuscript’s modelling implementation. Differences between the full manuscript-generating analysis chain and the main analysis are discussed in the audit with the author, but they are not treated as this sensitivity analysis.
The permitted data corrections and required comparison fields are fixed in manuscript_prepared_data_sensitivity.md. Both scenarios report the same exact fitted-model sample sizes and 95% confidence intervals.

title: Planned sensitivity checks
section: What this notebook uses and produces
text:
What this notebook uses and produces

Uses: the main H01–H11 results, the H01–H11 results obtained from the manuscript-prepared dataset, the placement comparison, the decisions about which metrics remain interpretable, and a table listing every planned alternative analysis.
Alternatives considered: 70%, 80%, and 90% coverage requirements; all near-eye records versus participant-days (one participant’s record for one calendar day) measured at both positions; complementary chest results; omission of sparse sites or one site at a time; justified alternative outcome distributions or transformations; alternative ways to represent repeated measurements and time dependence; and approved alternatives for gaps or state definitions.
Produces: the main-versus-manuscript-prepared-data comparison; sample counts for each additional alternative; and direct comparisons restricted to records shared by the main and alternative analyses. All comparisons report estimates with 95% confidence intervals; the exact participants, participant-days, time-resolved observations, and sites used by each model; model-fitting and distribution checks; influential-observation checks; warnings; and a conclusion about stability. Every comparison also reports the participants, participant-days or participant-level rows, one-hour or 30-minute observations where applicable, and sites shared by both models.
Fixed rules: change only one choice at a time; do not test every possible combination of alternatives; do not add temperature.

Each conclusion will be classified as:


stable when the conclusion and practical magnitude remain similar;

quantitatively sensitive when the conclusion remains but the magnitude crosses a practical threshold defined before the comparison;

qualitatively sensitive when the direction or statistical conclusion changes;

inconclusive when the available information does not support a clear conclusion;

invalid when the alternative analysis violates a required assumption; or

non-estimable when the model cannot estimate the requested quantity.
